i think dr. hirschauer's the goat!!! imma try to give as comprehensive of a breakdown as i can without getting bored and giving up on this review so bear with me please: exam 1 (on a monday i think): very representative of her problem sets. no surprises, nothing like that. i think acid/base was on this exam, so for that, i recommend using flashcards to memorize the functional groups + their pKas (she's so nice for having us memorize rounded pKas rather than the more accurate decimal) and then after you've got those down, search up a random medication/drug molecular formula image on google to see if you can identify the functional groups and their pKas (i credit the second recommendation to aubrey from gss lol). exam 2 (on a wed): iiiii didn't like this exam, not because it wasn't representative, but because this was personally my worst exam + this is when you really start learning orgo stuff according to her and praha (the ta). i distinctly remember praha telling us this exam is like 5 times harder than exam 1 (but don't let that scare you!! just overcompensate by studying more yessir). to this day, i hate substitution and elimination reactions (i only started feeling good about them during office hours held right before we took the exam), and stereochem is a little rough. looking back at my mistakes, though, a lot of them were kind of stupid or minor and those added up - it wasn't like i completely blanked on a whole question though. exam 3 (on a wed): technically this is the worst exam content-wise and tbh everything-wise... BUT no curveball questions imo. she curved this exam itself rather than adjusting the overall course curve (i think that's how it worked??). i uh studied for ~5 hours per day for the five days before the exam though and did maybe an hour per day of alkene reaction practice for the week or two before that. this unit genuinely sucks to learn though because you have to memorize what 14?? alkene reactions and a handful more alkyne reactions and yk... sometimes it feels like "what's the point in doing all of this" because dr. h would straight up say in class "yeah you kinda have to just memorize this stuff." for this unit, i recommend making your own summary sheet for all of the reactions, stating their name, mechanism (i tried to find patterns in these - e.g. three membered ring), anti/syn addition, markovnikov/anti-markovnikov addition, racemic product, etc. i thought her starter + challenge sets were great for mastering these b/c they literally just had you do each reaction with each molecule given. final: this one.. was kinda hard. not the worst, not the best. weird thing is my confidence level was similar to my exam 2 confidence, but i actually did well. unfortunately, i didn't go back to see my exam so i don't have much... ask dr. h for a breakdown on how much of each exam's content is on the final tho. for us it was like approximately exam 1: 20%, exam 2: 32%, exam 3: 32%, post-exam 3 (nmr): 20% or something i don't remember. other nice details about exams: - she has maybe like 5 ish? extra credit points on each exam which is nice - they're not all free per se, but they're not extremely hard at least. - exams usually get graded and grades posted within 2-3 days. - you can get your midterms back during discussion and keep them. for the final, she just announces a time for people to come view it - no pictures, no taking it home. grade cutoffs: dr. h posts an announcement with overall course grade cutoffs after each exam + stats like median for the exam + course. grade cutoffs tell you what the minus mark is (e.g. after exam 3 for us, an 86 was an a-, but we didn't know what an a was). note that for the final, she doesn't release grade cutoffs so no one ever knows how much you need at that point :( that made me stress quite a bit... welp. it's prob that the curve gets bigger though from what people say. homework: an elms quiz per week - 8 attempts per quiz. she says due saturday, but they're lowkey due sunday night to account for tech difficulties - just get it out of the way early though so that if you use up some attempts, you have time to ask her for help or at least to work at it some more. multiple select is annoying, but i won't complain because 8 attempts is beautiful. def possible to get 100% on all of them eventually even if some are a little harder. dr. hirschauer herself: really nice and funny! not as unhinged of a sense of humor as dr. hong, but she makes us laugh. tries her best to answer questions during lecture but sometimes can't. wish she could do more practice problems during lecture with us... but it's a time crunch with the syllabus. thus also goes kinda fast sometimes. she's really trying to convince the chem department to let her keep recording lectures with panopto, so please attend lectures or else you're just proving the dept right! her recordings are awesome for quick re-learning on your own when you feel like you're falling behind, esp during exam 2 and 3 content. our ta, praha: soooo a lot of people don't like him. but i do. whoops. he's kind of blunt/passive aggressive about stuff, but i think it's a good reality check... even if he tells us we didn't do as well on an exam as he'd expected since the exam was easier than normal... anyway he holds office hrs on zoom before each exam how to study: - do her problem sets for each chapter. starter sets and challenge sets too if she makes those available. if you can do those pretty solidly, you're in good shape. prob better if you work on them as she goes over the content in lecture - i started getting behind and would do them the week or two before the exam. some people ik would redo them before exams on top of that. - go to her office hours! if you can't make her normal time, shoot her an email the minute you find out (just get it out of the way at the start of the sem) saying you have a conflict and ask if she has any other availability. her office hours can get really full when you get to the week of or before the exam - i remember there were like 7 people in her office and maybe 7 more lined up outside before the final. nice thing is: she hosts extra office hours before each exam to give people more chances to ask questions. there's also a nice table outside her and dr. koppel's offices with a whiteboard where a lot of us would hang out and work on problems until we had a question for her. sometimes she'd come out of her office to help us there but only if there were a LOT of people. - ask questions during lecture if they come up or go up to her right after lecture ends. keeping a list of questions in my notes app helped me remember them all. might also help to sit closer to the front imo (i say this lightly but it is a STRONG recommendation if you get shy asking questions like i do). - go to gss sessions with alice and/or aubrey. i personally loved aubrey's worksheets (they were just cute okay -_-), but some people said alice posts harder problems. i honestly slacked off on attending these halfway through the semester, but i still kept doing the worksheets on my own since they're posted on elms. they have review sessions too, but i also uh never attended any except for the final due to schedule conflicts. the final review session was lowkey messy cuz they made mistakes, but they are usually quite good so let's cut them some slack yeah. go gss!! - praha's discussion worksheets are nice even if i didn't use them consistently - i recommend attending discussion cuz he's very straightforward about recommended studying tips + it's a more closer-knit setting to ask questions and he has more time to dive into the why of the chemistry that we're doing. - go to chem department problem solving sessions! this sem they were online via zoom thursday nights (9-10 pm). i got some nice tidbits from those - like what a nitro group looks like - and it's good to get extra practice + advice from different profs (the orgo profs take turns hosting these sessions). i also think if i went to the last one on nmr spectroscopy maybe i would've understood it better haha but it worked out okay for me. - get the organic chemistry as a second language book (first semester) by david klein - there's a free pdf online (alice and aubrey linked it on the gss page on elms) or you can get the physical copy (i liked the physical cuz it's a workbook so i could solve problems in it). nice supplementary material after you're done with dr. h's stuff or if you want to get ahead and preview content for future lectures. note that the first semester book does not cover ir/nmr/ms spectroscopy (that's in the second sem book) + doesn't have the oxymercuration/demercuration alkene reaction. might be missing a few other things, but honestly solid practice material. good luck - you've got this :)) WAIT I'M SO SORRY THIS IS SUCH A LONG REVIEW- if you know me irl you DON'T - BYE

Listen, chem lab will be chem lab, but I enjoyed this lab much more than gen chem. Go to the TAs office hours. My only thing is don't go to office hours without trying to do the work yourself. I do agree with others on this course being a lot of work for 1 credit but it's to be expected.

I found this lab to be pretty easy to follow in terms of doing the experiments. He has a bunch of helpful videos. Succeeding in this class is not difficult as the post-labs are completely reasonable. My only complaint is that studying for the practical was a bit difficult because there was a lack of communication about what material was going to be on the test. Additionally, he was completely unwilling to give any late credit on the quizzes so don't miss out on one them.

TLDR: Dixon's take on this course was pretty unorganized, which had positive (moving back dates of HW deadlines or exams if the majority of the class agreed, index card was allowed, & units were swapped around to match lab) and negative effects (typos, miscommunication, grading errors, lack of current study resources/old exams, & long HWs that feel extra compared to exam content). I listed more pros/cons below. Pros: Lots of office hours Can go to any discussion & TAs/resources were super helpful. They're sorta mandatory (idk). Sometimes attendance was taken, but other times it wasn't. Exam questions aren't necessarily tricky. They're just long. Some extra credit opportunities through HW & random email tasks. CAN (outside of lecture videos/Zoom) with extra practice. Lenient on deadlines if the majority of the class wanted a delay. For example, our Exam #1 was pushed back a class, and several HWs were also pushed back. Lecture content aligned well with the lab content, but that doesn't really matter because the lab has a lecture component. She goes over the question types and point breakdowns on the exam before the exam. An index card was allowed for the exams this semester. She seemed indecisive about whether she would keep them for future semesters. Cons: Lots of typos/mistakes in HW & sometimes exams. She often waits very long to announce them. Unclear about the purpose of the required asynchronous lectures. We had several, but only ended up getting tested on one or two topics from them. Crowded office hours. (This may just be a chemistry department problem because I think most of my other professors also had crowded OH) HWs are very difficult and feel too time-consuming for a 2-credit course. They seem to push beyond the understanding needed for the exams, which, according to the TAs, causes people to overthink the exams and fail. CANs aren't technically mandatory, but are essential to understanding HWs. Talks and takes notes kinda fast. No answer keys for old exams. No asynchronous worksheets with problems similar to exams. The CAN worksheets are more similar to HWs and are often used by her to clarify topics she didn't cover well in class that students kept asking about. Notes feel lacking in content. She's mildly straightforward and blunt. I can't speak too much about her personality besides a few email interactions I had with her, and I don't believe spreading other people's interactions I heard about would be the most accurate. Her clarifications in office hours are mildly confusing. She prohibits TAs from helping students with the HW, encouraging them to come to OH and work with others. She grades all the midterms herself. Surprisingly, she's pretty quick with it (Less than 1 week turnaround). My issue is whether she'll get fatigued and start grading differently for people despite similar mistakes, or make grading mistakes. I think the regrading process has been through asking her during office hours, which could lead others to hear the conversation. HW grading between TAs and the final score is very different. It seems to be a miscommunication issue between Dixon and the TAs. For example, my initial grade for HW #1 was a 11/15, then it got bumped to a 12/15. Then, Dixon regraded everyone's HW #1, and my grade became a 14/15. My grades were nearly 20% different from just grading issues.

Weird teacher if I have to be honest. Too worried about work life balance to actually care. Her lectures are useless for the lab so don’t go to those. Recommend to only go to TA office hours and the labs worksheets are time consuming and really poorly worded. Manageable after getting the hang of them and the exams are really fair. For the two exams just study the formula sheet and should be easy. Doesn’t disclose grades cause she gets overwhelmed by anything. Heard she’s nice though and the TAs are great.

Lectures were often broken up into 2 sections with a short break in the middle, and were always recorded with the slides being posted as well. I see a lot of people saying that he's monotone or lectures are boring, however I saw it more so as Pedram wanting to be as straightforward as possible when communicating content. Pedram and the TAs were also very responsive on Piazza for any questions that came up outside of class time. CS instructor (not professor, as he made very clear), yet no electronics are allowed any time in class. Not afraid to single people out if you leave lecture early. Assigned an exam immediately after fall break and immediately after thanksgiving break, so be prepared to study during all your breaks! Projects aren't so bad, but exams are pretty hard. One of the best professors I've had yet. I thought his lectures were well-paced, informative and easy to understand. He is an engaging and personable lecturer who takes time to answer questions and his participation system provides a nice padding to your overall grade if you happen to need that. The later projects were ROUGH but not impossibly difficult with a reasonable amount of effort, starting on them early is definitely for the best. His open note exams (which I greatly preferred) test your ability to apply concepts instead of memorize random details, for obvious reasons. I def think your grade reflects the amount of effort you put in, and honestly this class was much less stressful than 132 for me.

Even though I'm not a strong math student, I feel like I now have a firm grasp of this material, especially writing proofs. Fawzi made it very clear what you needed to know for the exams, and the grading was pretty relaxed. Overall, this was a great class and I'd recommend Fawzi for any class you can take with him. Max is an INCREDIBLY lazy professor. It truly feels like he puts in 0 time to preparing for lectures because his slides are often incomplete or a mess, he doesn't know the answers to any questions students ask during class (or he gives the vaguest hand-wavy response), and he frequently ends lecture 30 minutes early because he's run out of things to say. It feels like he himself doesn't fully understand what he's teaching sometimes. Like the other reviews note, he also fills a bunch of lecture time with unrelated thoughts and work stories, and while the class seems to find them entertaining (and Max loves the attention and reactions he gets from saying all his unpopular or taboo things), it would be better if there was more real content time to match. Max doesn't believe in studying any of the data science concepts rigorously, and while teaching a survey of topics at a high-level could be acceptable, he doesn't even touch on enough topics to make the class worthwhile. Instead, we learn in an entire semester basically what someone could get from reading a few articles on data science for a few hours. He also assigned multiple hours worth of youtube videos this semester in lieu of teaching the topics himself, and made the content directly testable on the exams. His reading-based exam questions (which constitute a significant portion of each exam grade) are genuinely trivia and not relevant to any fundamental understanding of data science concepts. He isn't active in responding to people's concerns on Piazza, mistakes are abundant in his posted materials, and policies seem to change frequently (such as him announcing a flat 11% curve on exam 1 then never following through on it). Overall I find it difficult to give a higher rating to a professor who transferred such little knowledge to his students and put in such little effort into his full-time teaching job. I excelled in this class (and you definitely can too) by always going to lecture, reviewing the slides carefully before exams, memorizing major points from the readings, and thinking critically about what Max must be looking for while answering exam questions.

Cliff and Anwar typically are the only people who teach this. Material is the same but definitely take Anwar over Cliff. Cliff's lectures are about as boring as can be. Imagine a theatre kid mixed with a introverted CS nerd. I would have rather watched paint dry than attend another one of his lectures as it would've been more entertaining and helpful than his lectures. His notes and slides are a mess filled with snazzy little transitions that make it a nightmare to navigate. The class overall felt pretty unstructured with random topics thrown in for the s and g's. At least Anwar recorded his lectures and explained things better than Cliff's philosophical mumbling. Material is difficult but certainly doable. Start project 5 early. TA's were hit or miss. I think there were maybe one or two good ones but the rest seemed to be pretty rude, unhelpful, or overall useless. My discussion TA was late half the time and spent most of the time arguing with one student about different ways to do problems. That's all I remember until I stopped showing up to the discussion at all.

Since I already had experience with web programming, this was one of the easiest CS classes I've ever taken. Nelson doesn't require attendance, so I showed up only for the midterms. He provides many resources to use when studying so you're never unprepared. One neat thing about the final project is it's up to you to design and implement it.

I found Ting's lectures very hard to follow. The slides presented information in a sort of confusing way, and her poor handwriting and strong accent made it a little hard for me to understand what was going on when we were getting into more difficult concepts. I ended up mostly using Justin's class notes and online resources because they were much easier to learn from. Since they co-teach, this worked out fine for homeworks and exams. If you, like me, are not a morning person, you are probably better off with Ting.

Computer architecture is not an exciting topic, and so her lectures are not the most exciting either. HOWEVER, she makes the most boring topics easy to understand and gives you plenty of practices for the material. She's very fair and accommodating. When we asked for an extension because of Election Day, she was willing to compromise. This is her first semester teaching I believe, and I truly truly truly hope Dr. Asgari will come back to teach another undergraduate CMSC course at UMD again. You will learn more than you thought you would about computer architecture if you take her.

Personally, I disagree with the one star reviews, I'd give her a solid 3 to 3.5 stars. I took this class Spring 2024, and I agree that she seems to care more about research than teaching, but I found her to be a really nice person and her teaching to be pretty clear and easy to follow. The projects were interesting to me and even though there were issues with submitting and a fair amount of disorganization, she gave extensions for the confusion and graded fairly in my opinion. I was able to get perfect or close to perfect grades on all four projects with a reasonable amount of effort. The exams were rough but the curve was generous and my final grade was an A even though I got 70s on the final and a midterm.

Professor Roy is really knowledgeable about networks and conveys the concepts well. Super interesting class, taught extremely well, and the lecture material is organized. On the other hand, I had a real issue with the projects. First off, the TAs are extremely unsympathetic to the workload you have while taking this class. It took an army to get hints on the test cases for each project. C programming and networking concepts related to programming are not taught in class at all, and you're forced to fend for yourself. At one point, the professor and TAs literally tell you to read a research article and implement it. The projects are designed well but need a serious overhaul in how test cases are run and how material is taught in class. If the professor didn’t feel like teaching the material for the projects, that’s fine—as long as there are decent guidelines and some starter code. This class had neither. The final project is very hard, but doable. It’s actually really cool to learn about, and you're given three other groupmates to complete it. Exams are fair. Lecturing is great. Projects are ass. (10–12 hours for the easy ones, and way more for the hard ones.) Two midterms, one final, five projects, and a final group project. I’m a senior now, and I don’t regret taking the class—but it was definitely the hardest class I've taken here. Godspeed.

Justin is a great lecturer who really makes the content engaging and easy to digest, and he posts great notes as well if you miss class. The seven exam structure was interesting, but I quite liked it. Given we had a midterm dropped and that the exams generally reflected the given practice material it was not too difficult to prepare for, and I found it less stressful to study one or two topics than studying a bunch of topics for two or three exams. Just start reviewing practice problems and making sure you understand how the exams DS works a couple of days before the exam and you should be good to go. The projects aren't too bad and have no secret test which is nice, and one is dropped. Great class, would recommend.

By far the best option you have for CMSC421 (though imperfect) Pratap is quite a nice lecturer. When looking at the slides at first (which, as AI is, is still stolen from Berkeley), some equations and concepts are kind of hard to grasp at first glance. But Pratap explains it in a simplified way while not removing the details fully. Although some of the AI concepts at the start are repetitive (BFS, DFS, and other stuff you learned), there's just enough to make the start somewhat different. Pratap records all his lectures (which lowers attendance drastically, but near the end of the semester, some lectures stopped being recorded for some reason. There were intended to be more assignments, but likely to disorganization, there were only 4 homework assignments and 1 lab. I really was hoping to do more coding (and the coding assignment was pretty easy, though these 5 assignments ended up being weighted up 10% each, crazy given the homework was also short). This may have happened due to disorganization, and really, disorganization is the main gripe I have with this class. TAs don't answer on Piazza, and Pratap answers nearly every question (I feel bad for him qwq). Homework grades come quite late, regrades are annoying, and questions are written strangely quite often. I feel that if this class were managed much better, it would be perfect, and strangely enough, more homework. Tests are easy. Like, really easy. The practice exam is extremely similar to the actual exam, so similar that it incentivizes overfitting on the practice exam (and, plus, you even have a cheatsheet for each test!). The averages were extremely high (87ish?) for each test, so that will not be a concern unless something changes. Overall, given the teachers I've seen teaching AI, be glad you have Pratap (though he's going on sabbatical...). Despite some flaws, he runs a good course for a notoriously poorly run class.

Prof. Carpuat seems like a very nice person, so I don’t want or intend to make personal criticisms or insults toward her — just share my experience with the class. First off, there is a lot of emphasis on memorization (even if she never directly admits it). It genuinely feels like the class is training us for a competitive memorization bee rather than machine learning. Instead of relying on memorization, there should be a broader and more diverse set of practice problems after each topic so students can actually understand and retain concepts through, you know, practicing. Students aren’t going to magically derive new ideas on the spot — especially not when the slides barely explain the material in the first place. If the foundational explanations are weak, you can’t expect students to perform theoretical acrobatics on an exam. The cheat sheet on exams isn’t really helpful either when you don’t know how to use it because the slides are bad. Am I supposed to analyze and figure out each slide on my own? Unfortunately, I can’t, because I have other classes and responsibilities (like job searching in this bad market). Also, the midterms are borderline impossible to finish on time; they feel like the SAT, except with fewer breaks and more panic. The point distribution is baffling: somehow a multiple-choice question can outweigh an open-ended one that requires actual reasoning. Grading is strictly “right/wrong,” and partial credit is treated like a rare mineral you have to mine via a regrade request on Gradescope. In regard to the TAs, they act as if they’re doing charity work by helping students or grading assignments. Guys, undergrads pay tuition. We don’t have funding or tuition remission like PhDs, so please take TA responsibilities seriously. The number of grading mistakes is honestly impressive in the worst way. And one TA is borderline dismissive toward students. Yes, we know you’re all busy revolutionizing research science with your “Einstein discoveries” and preparing your Silicon Valley IPOs, but TAing is still part of the job. Treating it like an unpaid internship doesn’t magically make it one. Her teaching style isn’t very effective. Every time she asks a question in class, it’s clear the majority of the room is lost. And while pre-class reading is important, the textbook she assigns does not clearly lay out the foundations of ML. She may think students are struggling because of the math, but that’s not actually the problem; the issue is the chaotic slides and unclear explanations. There’s an overwhelming amount of theory with very little practice to anchor any of it. Then there’s the SVM (or any other topic) situation. You’d expect a core ML topic to come with diverse practice problems. Instead, we get about 10 nearly identical questions across quizzes, problem sets, and practice exams. Same structure, same notation, same tiny subset of concepts. Meanwhile, the midterm features completely different SVM topics that only showed up in two or three theoretical slides. At this point, I genuinely can’t tell if this is intentional — like a way to force a “normal distribution” so fewer people do well — or just poor planning. The class is generally demotivating. You’d think that a course this central to AI would be taught with enthusiasm and would foster a real learning environment, but no. Instead, the class makes you feel like you’re not good enough because the focus is entirely on exams, not understanding. Why are there no projects? Because she’s convinced everyone will cheat using AI. Maybe instead of eliminating projects, design them so that AI isn’t enough to do the intellectual heavy lifting — just like in actual research, where a model spitting out code doesn’t magically produce hypotheses, perform data analysis, or make expert judgments. This class is just too much of emotional lifting, so I'm good with bare minimum of studying for the "right/wrong" final exam moving forward. I can't definitely go on with how disappointing this class has been but overall, the course doesn’t feel thoughtfully structured. It feels like something thrown together and held together with theory-heavy slides and a hope that students will just figure everything out on their own.

Very well-structured course where you are told exactly what is expected of you. He follows the textbook very closely and has detailed online slides. His grading is pretty good, sometimes a bit strict. Projects were relatively easy. Practice exams and homeworks were close to the actual exams. Second time taking this prof and would take a course by him again.

My friends told me that this professor knows he got a bad rating on this course and is planning to adjust the course material to make it easy for the next semester. He seems to plan to make everyone happy.

This has been one of the more interesting classes I've taken at UMD. It's very structured because the course format has stayed the same for many years (since Calderon taught it), but not much of that can be attributed to DVH himself if im being honest. The lectures were super useless, all they really involved were DVH going through tangential Racket code in his Racket REPL. Half the time, we would barely get through any of the topics in the lecture notes. That being said, the projects were really interesting for this class and the course notes are super helpful. A lot of these were created by Professor Calderon I think and they are super useful, and what made the class really rewarding in the end. If you take this class with DVH, I highly recommend checking out Jose's online videos / notes. They honestly were WAY more useful than going to DVH's lectures in my opinion. My experience with the TAs was definitely hit or miss. Some of the TAs were very sweet, caring, and helpful. We had really good response times on Piazza (shoutout Pierce!!), and some of the OH TAs were great and really caring. That being said, some of the TAs just felt underprepared and careless about the class. Sometimes, I felt that they didn't really know much about the projects or how to implement them, which made office hours unproductive for me on several occasions. The midterms were alright and felt very fair. DVH definitely does a good job making these, and gives very fair review materials and practice midterms. There are a handful of quizzes and surveys throughout the semester, but be careful not to miss them. I remember them being about 15% of our grade, and if you're even a little bit late, you get a 0 no exceptions. Overall, interesting course with some good material. But could be far more organized on the administrative end.

Please Please Please stay away from this professor. He makes the courses harder than it should be. TA's are not helpful because they don't even know it themselves. The professor doesn't help you either. You literally are left alone to die. Only take this course if you want to test hell.

I took CMSC434 with Golub this semester, which is probably a lot better to take with him than most classes (especially 351 or 250, that would've sucked). He wasn't by any means an outstanding professor, but he wasn't the worst that I have had either. He teaches reasonably, uses slides and posts the slide decks to ELMS. He made us participate by discussing with groups throughout the lecture, but participation wasn't worth a whole lot. As a grader, he came off as a bit nit-picky at times, but seemed reasonably understanding about giving extensions here and there. He can be heavy on semantics which can be a bit annoying at times. As for the class itself, 434 is a really interesting course that is rather unorthodox compared to most CS courses, and I enjoyed it more than I expected to. The class persists around things that seem to be common sense, but goes into plenty of detail. If you try to keep an open mind and think in depth about how the course knowledge would apply to some kind of software, you should be able to understand the course content easily. However, the structure of the class is also unorthodox, in that it surrounds a semester-long group project. This project is not consistently just coding, and is spaced out well that you should be fine as long as you and your group are dedicated. At times, Golub's grading can hurt you in this project if you aren't careful, so be diligent and read through all of the project requirements in depth. The class project is 46% of your grade, and the tests are 44%. There are four tests (including the final, however the final is not really a final and is worth the same percentage as the other three exams). The tests are where my biggest complaints are. They are entirely open ended, often 5 questions with an average of 2-4 subparts, totaling in around 15 or so paragraphs on average that you have to write. BY HAND! I had less hand cramps during the English section of the SAT, it really sucked. However, I was able to do generally well on the tests because the questions themselves were not hard as long as you studied. There were a couple exams where I ran out of time without being able to complete all of the questions. In summary: nice dude, can be a bit annoying with grading, project is extensive and sometimes hard, tests suck but not that hard. Overall: interesting class with a decent professor and okay execution.

Pretty flawed but also very chill. This course is extremely easy, with no exams or quizzes, defined as 6 labs only. The lectures are extremely useless, partly because there are no tests, partly because it's hard to go over them, but I also just didn't find Marsh to be a great lecturer. It's very hard to apply what he says and truly understand it, because there's no incentive to understand the deeper meaning behind Android development. It's extremely difficult, also cause slides have code, and things become extremely copy-pastable. All that is to say, nobody went to the lecture (as low as 5 people out of like 200?). Now, all of this is a good or bad thing, depending really on how much you care about learning, but I was hoping to at least learn a bit alongside the easy A. What did make me learn from this class, though, was Phase 4. There's an independent project separated into 6 phases, and the difficulty curve is insane (Phase 4 is harder than all the other 5 combined, IMO). While the first 2 are copy-paste, the last 4 get you to learn more, in my opinion, which is nice. Marsh alludes to Phase 4 taking a month... and he's kinda right? Don't procrastinate it, even with the flexibleish deadlines. Also, abuse the infinite resubmissions... Lastly (and least), there is the group project. I don't think the project itself is bad; it's rather lenient, pretty creative, and your ending result can be pretty cool! I'm somewhat biased because my group was pretty bad (please find a good group). It was a lot more stress, but most of the time, you'll be fine. If you want the easiest CS class possible, Marsh will be for you. Otherwise, it's a bit iffy depending on how much you really care about Android development.
This class was super hard, very difficult homeworks, some took me 30-40 hours, but you get 2 weeks to do them - START EARLY Overall it was a good class, i learned a lot, it was hard asf tho....
Really chill professor. First two exams and final were very similar to the practice exams, although exam 3 was slightly harder. Homework was challenging, but not impossible and interesting.

I do not agree with this professor's approach to teaching this class. Oftentimes materials were poorly explained/glossed over in lecture, as he read mostly off the slides then went on tangents about how he worked at Google or how you can make a lot of money in big tech (ugh). Assignments were released far in advance, but the material on the assignments was often taught much closer to the due date, making the actual window to complete them much lower if you didn't want to flip through lecture slides from 3 weeks out. He expects you to teach yourself a lot of the material to be able to perform on projects and exams, which makes some sense for the real world, but he was unforgiving and not understanding in my communication with him, seeming dismissive of my difficulty with the class. Oftentimes he would point to external materials to build "problem-solving" skills for the course, which were graduate level course recordings on his YouTube channel, which were confusing and convoluted to my feeble undergrad brain. We also received grades nearly a month after homeworks/exams were completed which increased my salt levels a bit. If you have trouble teaching yourself a good chunk of a course, then I would not recommend this professor, since it's an expectation that you not only show up to lecture and take notes, but also put in multiple hours making sense of difficult external materials to get to the level he expects. It's a shame this class was managed the way it was, because I found the material we were learning very interesting when I actually understood it, but this class was definitely a trip on the struggle bus for me. Maybe the C- "recommendation" in CMSC351 (which is a requirement for the CS degree so idk why that's a recommendation when it's required) should be raised to B+ or A- so that people understand how smart you should be to succeed in this class with Prof. Hajiaghayi.
Homework was a bit challenging sometimes, but it really helped me understand the content better. Contents are lengthy but I found them quite helpful.

Aric is a very nice person and tries to get to know all of his students and finds interest in them. I truly believe that I learned a lot from this class, but in the least efficient way possible. His class is a completely in-person class, but if I want to know the information and do well on the exams, I need to watch the lecture videos he assigns, which took me an average of 2 hours a week outside of class alone. He is one of the most disorganized professors I have had, and it becomes evident in very important situations. There's a group project at the end of the semester that is so rushed and is just an addition to continuing with everything else we have been doing the rest of the semester and the expectations of how much he wants us to include in it are unreasonable. If you take his class, which I think you could learn a lot from, be prepared to devote a lot of time to it outside of class and be forced to create your own organizational system for his class because he does a terrible job at doing that himself.

I'm not entirely sure as to why Professor Duffy has good reviews. She is such a boring professor. All she does is reads off slides, and speaks in such a monotone manner. Her lectures are not interesting and simply mimic what is spoken in the video quizzes. I preferred Professor Diker over her, but unfortunately, she teaches most of the course. She put more effort into reporting half the class for being in a GroupMe than to ensuring her lessons are engaging. If you are able to, do not take Professor Duffy for this class. She's not worth the mental and academic stress.

MATH140– Literally the worst, nice person but awful teacher. Class avg for the first exam was a 30, and from there on was around a 60, which is not good. Multiple times in class, she essentially called us stupid for not being able to opt out of the class due to not getting the AP credit etc. She would also single out kids who asked questions, and would answer their questions with a response that was formulated to make them feel stupid. Class was around 150 students, and after the first 2 weeks, around 20 kids showed up consistently to class, since her teaching was a joke. If you can, DO NOT TAKE HER.

I was scared going into Calc 2 as everyone said it was a weed out class but Professor Song was great. Exams were similar to problems solved done in class and she would tell us what would be on the weekly quizzes. Id say a better option for Calc 2

If you're taking linear algebra(especially as a freshman), I highly reccomend that you DO NOT take this professor. I know his ratings are good, and that's because he isn't a bad teacher, he knows what he's doing, but he goes extremley fast in lectures. His percentage distributions are terrible, the final is 30 percent of your grade, and math finals are normally pretty difficult. The midterms are tricky as well, other teachers like Shin Song have much easier midterms. Taking this class as a freshman was draining, I studied so much to end with a B. The concepts in this class aren't hard, but the tests he gives make it hard. I reccomend taking another professor who is more lenient with their exams.

Williams is an amazing lecturer but his exams required a level of understanding that was incredibly difficult to grasp with the given practice and pace of the class. Unless you are naturally very smart I wouldn't recommend taking him. I had to spend unholy amounts of time to keep up in this class, which definitely hurt my ability to do well in my other courses. He is adamant that his exams reflect the suggested problems in the textbook, but I found that was only slightly true for a few of the harder word problems in the textbook. He's not the absolute worst professor to get, especially if you happen to have a lighter course-load and dedicate most of your time to this, but if I were to take the class again, I would take another prof who has more reasonable exams and go to Williams' lectures. If you absolutely have to take him, make sure you have full fluency for all the suggested word problems (like you should basically have the problems and solutions memorized). I'm not sure how, but if you can, try to learn how to do the math as quickly as possible since the hardest part of him exams is having to know what to do immediately with how little time you have for so much work. When you understand them, the math you have to do for his exam problems isn't crazy difficult, it's just that the way he phrases them is so convoluted that you're going to spend more time trying to decipher them than actually doing math on the exam. Just prepare to be severely humbled by this class, he's a great guy but his course was psychological torture

I think Dr. Doucette was a great teacher and is going to be even better when you take her because of her constant goal to receive our feedback and improve. Admittedly, at the start of the semester her lectures were a bit rough because she was using the chalkboard in a classroom where it was hard to see, and she was kinda all over the place and explained certain concepts too much before doing examples. She overcomplicated a lot of things. However, she consistently asked for our feedback, so she switched to a projector, started doing more examples, and she became more confident in how she explained things, and I ended up finding her lectures super helpful. All I had to do was examples from the textbook to study after getting the basis of each topic down from her lectures. She gives weekly discussion quizzes but they're free because she sends an announcement and describes the exact type of question she's gonna ask on it, so as long as you do practice problems to study beforehand you'll do fine. She also dropped 2 quizzes. I found these helpful for keeping up with the content, as every quiz was basically just one exam-type problem, so by the time the exam comes you've already done each type of question. Her exams were super fair for the most part; the first exam was exactly like the practice exam she had given us and the third exam was easier than the practice exam she gave us. The only exception was exam 2, which was honestly a lot harder than I expected but I still did good (almost every niche thing you'd assume she wouldn't include on it, she did, like the dirac delta and heaviside functions for laplace and also a pretty hard version of undetermined coefficients). Her exam averages were 90.2, 76.4, and 84.9 for exams 1, 2, and 3 respectively. Overall she's a sweetheart and I highly recommend!!

FR THE GOATTT!! I understood proofs so much because of him and his lectures were super interactive which made me grasp the concepts more. He's genuinely the nicest professor I have ever had and cares a lot about his students. Would recommend to everyone if you have the opportunity to take a class with him please please do it you will not regret.

Junyan is the goat. Seriously, he explains concepts soooo nicely and really does right by the students. He moved up our final so we didn't have to take it the day before graduation, allowed us cheat sheets on exams, gave us a breakdown of the topics that could appear on the exams, and was in general nice. If you take MATH401 with him, note that a lot of the content was repeated from MATH240/461, so it was really slow in the beginning, but eventually we got to new stuff like 2/3 of the way into the semester. Oh, but the 50 min classes? Yeah that time crunch for the exams is definitely noticeable, so just know your stuff down well. I recommend Junyan.
rosenberg is my goat, prep as much as possible for the second midterm because it will be HARD
Homework was obnoxiously lengthy but later on some problems became optional. Used an unusual textbook and I feel like we learned less than other 405 classes overall

very hard class. i took it in the summer. there are 10 homework over 6 weeks so around 2 homeworks per week. they take pretty long. exams are hard. however the professor is great and he knows what he's talking about. he is also very nice, pretty chill guy. if you have any struggles in the class, just reach out to him. he also adds a nice curve at the end, but don't rely on it.

He is super understanding and probably one of the most relaxed and laid-back professors I have ever had. There is hardly any graded work for the class, but everything is super confusing, and he expects you to do a lot of self-exploration if you really care about the subject. I wish I could take him again if I have the chance.

Don't take with this professor. He grades very harshly for exams which make up 20% of the course grade each with a uniform distribution of scores around 50%, and he does not spend the time going over what he should expect for writing proofs.

For this class, he's honestly a really good lecturer. He explains how things came to be and why things matter, which is always a good thing when introducing left field concepts. So I enjoyed his lectures a lot. Overall the class is pretty straightforward in the content, as his lecture notes span maybe 30 or 40 pages for the entire course (of course, they are not fully complete). He also allows for students to make up grades with an extra-credit project worth around 10%, but the project comes with very high standards. The exams are what I call "troll": as a veteran student of mathematics they consist of various little tricks which are decently easy to see if you are decently mathematically mature and which seem intractable if you are not, which is why the exam averages are 60-70%. Overall the course is interesting and I would recommend people take it for an elective or something like that.

Every review about Beuhrle is kinda right. He's a really nice guy, and his lectures were actually quite interesting. He was always readily available by email, and communicated exactly what was expected of us in class. He always recorded lectures, and posted the slides, so actually going to lecture wasn't necessary. There was a weekly homework assignment that took around 3-4 hours, and was really your best bet for studying for the exams. There were also weekly quizzes that were entirely conceptual, and took about 10 minutes. Apart from that, the lab section of this course was entirely unrelated and just a grade booster (worth 20% of your grade). The exams were HARD, and I mean like everyone failed hard. We consistently had 20-40% curves on the exams, with your lowest score being dropped. Overall, if you already know basis physics you will do well in this course, and he isn't a bad choice!

Ouch this guy is so outta whack. Do your GPA a favor, take someone else. His exams are all over the places. If your physic is semi ok, you'll feel like crap when taking his exams. I don't understand why he doesn't write his own exam that is related to what's teaching in the classroom, but instead he takes some questions from college board website, probably copy and paste and said he wrote them. At the end of the class, I think he curved like 1% or something geez.

Buerhle is an enthusiastic professor who you can tell has an obvious love for physics from the first day of class. His teaching style is pretty straightforward, but he explains concepts in such an oddly simplified way that seems almost rehearsed. Then again, he constantly reminds us that he's an astrophysicist trying to connect with all these bio and pre-med folk so I guess you can cut him some slack? Personally, everything was a bit much for me, from TopHat readings (long but for completion), ExpertTA (supposedly for completion...you have to get the right answers to complete assignments but you don't always have to show your work depending on the question), answering graded "starred" questions during lectures (basically Clickers where you answer the question based on accuracy - ultimately forcing you to have to go to each lecture since you can't see the question from your own device and can't anticipate when he'll put up a starred question), to getting through each lecture fully understanding what was going on. The class is a flipped classroom (learn outside of class, apply during lecture) which I never like, regardless of the class I'm taking. tl;dr Structured lecture and teaching, but engagement is a give or take Lab was NOT structured. It was mostly "look at the supplementary docs on ELMS and do it". You'll be using ImageJ for every single lab and let me tell you that thing is so outdated. Lab reports were long, long, long and painful, especially if you didn't know what was going on. Barely related to what we did during lecture. So yes, be thankful for the exam curves, your lowest dropped exam, "curved" lab scores (which for us was thrown into one overall lab grade last minute as "normalized lab scores"), and your front-and-back cheat sheet but keep in mind that the final determines your absolute final grade. No curving after all that. Anyway, try to stay focused because that'll probably be the biggest challenge, but passing is definitely doable.

The class itself is hard but Severson curves based on a standard curve, has practice exams and records class. Participation credit is open for 24hrs so you don't have to go. The lab sucks but that's just phys lab. ExpertTA HW each week. I don't think you get options for a phys class for bio major but regardless he's aight. Also has a couple of dropped tophat questions. Cheat sheet for test but tbh the material is hard and there's so much that it's hard to prepare well. That said exams don't count for everything in this class.

I don't understand why professor Girvan has a low rating on this website. Yes the content in this class is confusing and the averages on the exams are low but she is an amazing lecturer. She is very good at answering questions during class and is great at pointing out the key parts of example problems as she goes through them. She did ok at making the lectures interesting but with them being so long its hard. Her exams are somewhat difficult but you are allowed to create your own large note sheet with whatever you want on it. She provided a strange curve at the end of the course which was: A+: ≥ 96, A: 90–95.99, A-: 86–89.99, B+: 80–85.99, B: 75–79.99, B-: 70–74.99, C+: 65–69.99, C: 60–64.99, C-: 50–59.99, D: 40–49.99, F: < 40. BSCI410 is designed to introduce advanced topics and techniques by building off of concepts from courses like BSCI222. While I believe that BSCI410 topics are harder to grasp than BSCI222 topics, Dr. Wu is highly supportive of her students and makes the class much more manageable. She is easy to approach, enthusiastic about the subject, loves to answer questions, and will go out of her way to supply her students with in-depth responses to questions. Additionally, to stress the importance of understanding material over memorizing it, Dr. Wu makes her exams open-note. Lectures can be rather dense at times, but the slides are explained clearly during class and broken down into simpler explanations. In terms of the actual content taught in BSCI410, a recurring theme is applicability. Dr. Wu structures the course to cover aspects of biology that students can actually apply to careers in biology and genetics. This includes introducing commonly used techniques and methods as well as experimental designs and analysis. A recent development for the course that I appreciated was the introduction of bioinformatics assignments. As an increasing amount of research relies on RNA sequencing, proteomics, etc, having the skills in R to create graphs and interpret data is vital. I would argue that this class has more assignments (homework, short essays, quizzes, etc) than most of my other upper level BSCI classes, but they aid in understanding and give you additional practice. To help students outside of the lecture and office hours, Dr. Wu encourages students to ask questions on the class Piazza. Whether it is for homework, classwork, exams, or just curiosity, TA’s and Dr. Wu provided thorough replies in a timely manner. Overall, I would highly recommend taking BSCI410 with Dr. Wu. You will learn a lot, gain relevant skills, and be a part of a collaborative environment.

I am shocked to see so many people up in arms about the high number of midterms in this class. It seems like I am in the minority when I say I didn't mind this structure and actually kind of liked it. Justin changed his CMSC420 course structure this semester to be very largely exam-based, with a "midterm" exam every two weeks. He did this with the idea that if he assigned homework, students would just ChatGPT the whole thing (and he's probably not wrong). At surface level, this does sound atrocious and I was worried at first. But there is a pro to this structure: there were no major midterm exams that required cramming a huge amount of content into your brain, like most classes. Each exam was entirely focused on the material we had covered since the last exam, which was at max two weeks, or five lectures, of material. Thus, there was only so much he could possibly test on, making studying easier (for me at least). The rest of the things that people have praised Justin for over the years haven't gone away: his super engaging lectures, his detailed and organized notes, and his stellar focus on helping students succeed. For every topic we covered, he had a set of organized optional problems on that topic available on ELMS. Before each exam, he would post on Piazza which questions within those problem sets to focus on when studying. So my studying usually consisted entirely of working through those suggested problems, which was enough to get me As on just about every exam. Maybe the material just clicked with me in a way that it didn't for others, but I had to study for like maximum two hours for each exam. As such, I actually liked this structure because for me, it kept the workload outside of class pretty light. Study for an exam one night every two weeks, do the occasional project here and there (these were pretty straightforward, enjoyable, and well-explained). He also drops the lowest exam grade and lowest project grade, so there's a nice cushion for error there too. I'm not sure if he will keep doing this in the future, because he has seen the negative feedback here and elsewhere and has acknowledged that he wasn't aware some students would have such major stress in regards to this class. TL;DR: If you are a student who tends to study a LOT for exams and tends to get really stressed before exams, I would stay away from this class with Justin, because you'll probably fall into the same hole as a lot of these 1-star reviewers. But if you're someone like me who doesn't stress too much over exams, I imagine this class will feel light for you too. Justin is still a top-notch lecturer and professor, and I loved learning this content from him.

loved taking cmsc421 with Pratap. him teaching it definitely made it the favorite upper level cs class that i've taken at umd. slide decks are structured very well and provide a ton of information, all of which i found really interesting. homeworks and projects are very interesting to work on and he provides practice exams for his exams, so you know what to expect on exams and can prepare really well for them. 10/10 experience for me and would highly recommend taking cmsc421 with Pratap to anybody.

I don’t understand where the positive comments about the class structure are coming from. Yes, ELMS is organized, but the lectures and homework don’t actually help with understanding the material (the class relies mostly on Eastern-style rote memorization). Her exams are unreasonably difficult, and the grading is extremely harsh; even small mistakes are treated as "fatal". It feels like she expects undergrads to perform at a graduate level. I didn’t get much out of this class and wouldn’t recommend taking it with her.

This was the most difficult class I've ever taken at UMD, and I do not know why it was necessary for it to be this way. The participation quizzes in lecture are grading on accuracy, the reading quizzes during the week are difficult, and the exams are absolutely brutal. Avoid this professor at all costs and take another semester to actually enjoy learning about databases instead of tearing your hair out.

Probably one of the worst classes I've taken so far. Lectures are very high level so they give you limited guidance on how to do the projects, making the class almost entirely self guided. And the professor often goes on random tangents about unrelated topics. Would not reccomend...

DVH is alright. Good lectures with plenty of dry humor. Projects are hard outside of the first two but manageable so long as you get started early. Helpful TAs on Piazza (shoutout Pierce). Easy quizzes/surveys, and access to some excellent notes which can supplement lecture. My main problem is how disorganized things are, deadlines are set but rarely met, when he says something will be out Tuesday expect it to be on Thursday or even later. Also no late credit if you turn things in late. If you enjoy this class check out CMSC838E with DVH, the grad level version where you go even more in-depth into these very same topics.

PROS: - course content is not difficult; the sheer amount of assignments is what makes the class difficult - Professor Li is VERY responsive on Piazza. Between the professor and the TAs, posts usually don't sit unanswered for more than a few hours. Same goes on weekends too, though maybe a longer response time - Lectures are recorded and are posted to elms with the slides - online + open notes exams CONS: - Each week you'll either have 2 or 3 things due or nothing due. If there's nothing due one week there's a big project due the following week. - Your learning will come from the TAs office hours and learning on your own because the lectures provide little to no educational value. - His accent makes things impossible to understand. Horrible professor that doesn't know how to teach. Just tells stories all class that have nothing to do with the exam. Grading on projects is harsh and subjective and descriptions are very vague. It's an easy class but it's an overall headache.

I loved this class! I have never taken or done app development, but I enjoyed it a lot. The lectures are kind of pointless since most of the phases require you to learn on your own, but I guess that's normal for a 400 level class. The class consisted of two overall projects (an individual one and a group one). The individual one was 6 phases where you work towards creating an app. The grading system is really nice in this class, since you can submit as many times as you like (can keep improving your grade) as long as you get the final product (phase 6) in on time. The due dates listed are suggestions, which I highly recommend that you follow. The group project was basically any app you want to make with some features that require outside of class knowledge (it's pretty simple to find one). There are no exams or quizzes, just projects. The TAs sometimes answer on Piazza, they just randomly decide to ignore the one question I need answered (;-;), but ig they're trying their best. Although this class did require a lot of effort it was enjoyable and it was nice to see a class where I am more focused on learning the actual development than stressing about an exam where I got to memorize a bunch of things :D

Going into this class knowing it was going to be a shit show prepared me well. He made the midterm into hws which was dope. He also split the final into an in person and a take home. As long as you go to at least one lecture a week you should be fine.

Very nice guy and funny. Willing to help with problems and questions. Made the first 2 exams very easy and similar to the practice exam, but threw a curveball for exam 3, it was harder. The homework is tough but the entire class is just homework and exams with some free in class quizzes every Friday that you can work on with others.

Prof. Hajiaghayi is great. Enthusiastic, good lecturer, and responsive to questions. Lectures feel like a math class with definitions and theorems. Projects are hard and require learning stuff not taught in lecture, but assigned very early (1+ months) and are very applicable to computational game theory. HWs are easy and straightforward. Grading includes 2 in class quizzes, a midterm and final (with midterm replaced with final if it improves your grade), 4 HWs, and 3 projects. You'll learn a lot.

I agree with others that there’s a lot of content for just 1 credit, but honestly, the slides helped a lot and the homework really made me learn the material. I actually feel good about what I got out of it.

Too much content to learn outside of class, more time should be spent introducing material in class instead of going over virtual lectures that have been assigned for a class that is neither hybrid nor online. Cool person though, just really annoying amount of online lecture content and weird due dates
Easy class, just make sure your group for the semester long project doesn't procrastinate and you'll be good

TAKE HIM. Does not prepare you that well for the final but your grade in the class will be so good (Mine was 95) that it does not matter. The midterms are EXACTLY LIKE THE PRACTICE TEST. You should get 100. My friend somehow got an A- in the class by getting a 93 on the final but that was insane because his grade was so low before. AND he curves. Good lecturer but is an awful grader, no curving exams or final grades. Low 70s averages with class average being in the 70s, with many kids stressing for the final to even pass the class (with a C).

Professor Wong is an elite professor. You learn so much from him and he clearly is like one of the most knowledgeable people you'll ever meet when it comes to math. His lectures are fast-paces but it doesn't really feel rushed or that you aren't up to speed with the material. I also think he covers some extra topics (not on the final) at the end of the semester to talk about the important of Linear Algebra which I found was quite interesting and unique, showing just how much he cares about students understanding why they are taking the course and their practical applications in the real world. There are weekly quizzes, but they are the easiest quizzes you'll ever take. He essentially tells you exactly what is going to be on the quiz, and the TAs cover those topics before you take the quiz. For me, I pretty much never studied for them because they were so easy and straightforward. Discussion was extremely valuable. the TAs are really smart and explain things in a phenomenal manner. If you have any questions about literally anything, you can just ask them and they will help you out. As for exams, Professor Wong is very clear is what is going to be covered. There are never any trick questions, but the exam is very theory heavy. Be sure to understand what you're actually doing because there are a lot of T/F questions and others that test your actual understanding, not merely following a pattern to compute things. He also provides practice exams and they are pretty similar for what you would expect for the exams. I didn't really have to study much for the exams because it was all very straightforward and Professor Wong and the TAs really give you everything you need to success. I would say the final was definitely harder than the midterms (which is expected), so definitely study hard for it. But very reasonable and follows a similar structure and pattern to previous exams which are all given. Overall, I couldn't recommend a better professor for 240. As a CS major, you actively learn some of the applications of Linear Algebra and learn a lot from Professor Wong.

Junyan was not great for me; he doesn't assign any mandatory homework, so it was hard to stay on top of the course material weekly. The lectures were pretty difficult to understand, especially if you couldn't get a seat in the first three rows of the lecture hall (partially just bc the armory sucks tho). My TA, Waldman, definitely saved me in this class; his assignments were relevant, and his quizzes weren't bad. Another downside was Junyan's curve SUCKS. He communicated it very poorly, and our average final grade was definitely lower than that of most other professors. Overall, I would recommend another professor for people who are new to calc 3. She doesn’t do a very good job with lectures. They are kind of hard to understand and over complicates some stuff. She does have lecture summaries that are helpful if you miss class or something. Her tests are very easy and she does care a lot about her students, but her tests are so easy that when it comes to the final that she doesn’t write, you are very unprepared. The class average for tests were significantly lower than the final, around 15% lower. If you take her, don’t take her tests as a baseline for how the final will be.

Dr. G is genuinely, without a doubt, the best math professor I have ever had at UMD. The sheer amount of kindness and care that he has for us is astounding, and I do not have enough kind words to say about him. I have never felt so welcomed in a classroom before, and despite the course being an introduction to higher level math topics, there was not a single topic that I was confused about, because Dr. G's lectures were at an extremely reasonable pace and unbelievably helpful. In addition to his calm and friendly demeanor, he lectures in a clear and concise way, ensuring all students have a firm grasp on topics and he makes sure of this. Overall, if I could choose to take him for every single math class I will ever take in the future, I would.

Severely underrated professor. While teaching may be boring at times, her practice exams prepare you very well and assignments are semi-interesting. Assignments/exams are more than fair and this professor is extremely kind/understanding. She is also very responsive to questions! Only thing is grading speed, but thats usually how it is in smaller upper level math classes. Loved having her as my 401 professor and would recommend anyone else to take her.

Professor Conway was great for MATH403. This class was very interesting and challenging, and professor Conway was very supportive of our learning. Multiple grading options were provided for this class, with the one that gave you the best score determining your grade. The standard grading option was 20% HW, 50% midterm exams (25% each), 30% final exam. Pros: - Very good lecturer: Went through all the details of theorems and gave plenty of examples. I never felt anything was unclear. - Good homework: The HW problems were relevant and challenging. There were 9 HW assignments in total but I always felt there was plenty of time to complete them. Lowest two HW grades are dropped. - Fair exams: The exams were all pretty fair. All the material in exams was covered in lecture. While they were pretty hard, it was representative of the overall difficulty of the course itself. The exams were graded relatively quickly as well. - Posts notes and lectures on ELMS: All of the content that the professor covers is on ELMS. If you miss something in lecture, you can always rewatch it online. - Personable and friendly: Very willing to help and answer any type of question. Clearly very invested in the students and the course content. Listens to student feedback and adapts. Cons: - Nothing comes to mind. Overall, I highly recommend Professor Conway for MATH403.

I loved this class, every second of it. It's really tough, and it will make your inductive reasoning skills really strong. I did horrendously on the majority of the exams however due to, well, a poor understanding of the course. Dr.dilllery would often say that so long you don't cheat on the Hw you should be able to do the exams, and this is true to some extent since a majority of exam problems are often taken from the homework, or inspired by them. Its important that you know how to do these problems properly however otherwise you'll end up probably failing like me. Often stack overflow would contain answer to these HW problems and would explain how to do them in detail. He says to ask him for help directly if you end up getting stuck, which provides a more healthy experience with solving the problems. Dillery himself is a professor who comes off as authoritative at first, but is really altruistic towards his students and generous. He's always willing to help his students with nearly anything. In general though, this class attracts some of the smartest students UMD has to offer in my opinion. Just getting to sit there is an honor. This is the only class that I'm honestly okay with absolutely failing, I'm glad I took it anyways.

Peter Dillery is a top-tier lecturer, but the organization of his class is a little lacking. His homeworks are difficult but reasonable, and his exams are never too difficult. Overall, I'd recommend him.
He's the best! And he graded our exams in a day one time so we could decide to add/drop that weekend. Goat.

Maybe the lectures are a little slow, but he is very knowledgeable and clearly cares so much about teaching the course well. Is also always trying to get people to engage and ask/answer questions. Pretty easy exams, and homework is mostly easy problems from Fitzpatrick. Highly recommend if you want to really learn this stuff. Really great professor!

Her lectures are pretty fast paced, but i love that she uploads her notes so quickly. He was not very good at conveying information for the course. Boring lectures. Thick accent. I learned from the book. Big curve though.

this class is 100% done on prior knowledge, tbh i never stepped foot in the lecture hall and i have a high A before the final. every exam is curved sm that u dont need to study. plus the cheat sheet is clutch.

prof is chill, make sure you do the clickers. class is 'mandatory' because of the clickers. exams are annoying but the curve is insane. for the second exam, a 75 was curved to a 93-ish. decent professor but rlly boring lecture, he loves his work but the content in class and the content on the exams are very irregular and don't match up.

One of the best professors I've had at UMD. This professors research focus is physics education, and it shows in her educational ability. She even takes a couple classes to focus on future career interests, and is willing to help students with that part of their college lives.

This professor is a no-nonsense professor. His notes just get straight to the point. His notes are also very clear and excellent. His tests are no-nonsense. Good luck to those who have not had this guy for 401.

I've had Prof. Shawhan for two different courses, PHYS171 and PHYS410, and I can say that he is one my most favorite professor I've had here at Maryland. He truly does challenge you to think, and not just mechanically produce an answer. He posts all the notes, which are extremely good by the way, online. Always has tests reviews, weights heavily on homework (which is nice), and truly wants you to understand the material. Very easy class and exams are exactly like old/practice ones. Attendance is mandatory at all lectures and discussions though.
Lectures are just reading off textbook definition. However, he is nice and answers to quizzes are given before taking it.

Absolutely amazing professor, the other reviews basically sum everything up. I liked how he taught the course in a more theoretical way as it made the content very interesting. Overall I had a fantastic experience in STAT401 with Professor Gaffi and I hope to take other classes with him if he decides to teach them! Definitely take him if you can

READ FOR DETAILS I was debating writing this review or not, but I decided that it was worth writing. Overall, he is an alright professor. He is not the best lecturer, and his lecture notes are impossible to read, but he goes rather slowly and you can very easily keep up by following the course online with YouTube lectures. He gave one midterm, then cancelled the second one and moved all its weight to homework. This naturally caused grades to spike in the class. To make up for this, he gave a really awfully hard final that we were not prepared for at all (no practice, just told to review the homework. Spoiler alert, it was nothing like the homework.) I literally opened that final and couldnt answer a single question. The average was a 23, with a high of 65, so every single person failed that final. However, I will contest the current one star rating. I do not think he is deserving of this at all. I am rating him 5 stars not because he is a 5 star teacher, but because 1 star is just unfair. If I would rate him, I would give him a 3.5/5 for the following reasons: Pros: - Very kind and reasonable guy who is willing to try to explain anything and can accommodate almost anything - Tries to make the class manageable - Homeworks are pretty easy - Grades very generously Cons: - Lectures are hard to follow because of his thick accent, and his handwriting is impossible to read which makes his notes useless - Gave a curveball final that everyone failed, which was not a good call but honestly I get why since the average grade in this class was >95% before the final... Overall, if you take him, I expect him to change up his teaching style massively next time he teaches. This was his first semester here I believe. I found the following YouTube series very helpful for this course, and would highly recommend regardless of what professor you end up taking: - Probability Theory (Bright side of Mathematics) (Good overview of general theory) - Intelligent Systems Lab probability playlist (good visuals) - jbstatistics (Goes over pretty much everything in an approachable manner, really demystifies a lot of the stuff) - 3blue1brown (Amazing visuals and good for selected topics to develop intuition)
Just bad in every way. If you actually want to learn something, don't waste your time.
Does what a professor should do in a class, is easy and you learn what is necessary. Assignments are online.

Dr. G is genuinely one of my favorite professors here at UMD. As a first year handling the transition from high school to college, Dr. G really helped me figure things out. I want to point out that if you do bad on the first exam, you can get an A. I am living proof. Although it took a TON of work to make it, I managed to claw my way from a 75% after the first exam to a 90% after the final. Dr. G is genuinely helpful and cares about student success. Yes, she doesn't drop the lowest midterm but who can blame her, it creates magical thinking that you are invincible (you are not). Review her study guides thoroughly and PLUG THEM INTO CHATGPT FOR QUESTIONS. Her office hours are the most resourceful thing you can do. Super helpful and super in-depth. Make concept maps, I did one for each lecture and it made everything so manageable. I had a really good upward trend of exam scores after using concept maps. After the first exam (F), I got As on every exam after, and an A+ on the final. The lectures are super organized and she records them and uploads them to Canvas. Her exams are very very very conceptual, NOT memorization. Highly recommend taking her!
Such a horrible lab. I can't even describe how outrageous the workload was. There are never any clear directions pn how to complete individual projects and you're completely left in the dark.

Pretty awesome guy. Unlike other professors, he understands that you have other classes and commitments. So, while he assigns a fair number of assignments, you only need to do a few and the rest are dropped. Also, he teaches at a very high level and tells you what specifics you need to know for the class and what isn't as relevant. His study guides are also a great place to start as they are quite thorough. Very low-effort class, you can put in little effort and still do well.

Josh is the best TA I have ever had. He makes sure you actually understand the concepts. These new reviews are unfair. Yes, her lectures are not very thrilling but anatomy is a hard class because it is an information dense class. She tells you what you need to know during lecture and her exams are very similar, if not, identical to her lecture slides. She tells you the trick questions that will show up on the exam in class and then the correct answer to these trick questions. She also provides an exam review sheet that is almost identical to the exams and she goes over the answers in the lecture before the exam. So yes, while BSCI201 is extremely information heavy and it is a memorization based class, she provides you with all the resources you need to succeed in the class.
