I loved Dr. Lombardi! The material was really interesting and she taught it in a way you could understand! I got an A on each exam, but I put in work to study. I can see how the exams would be difficult if you didn't have a good study technique down. This class is mainly MEMORIZATION!!! I basically turned every lecture topic into quizlets, and some of my quizlets are 200-300+ terms. She teaches the conceptual info really well, and sometimes I wouldn't get it the first time in a lecture and would be able to get it on my own with the slides or a quick youtube video. She recorded her lectures which was really nice for if you couldn't come to class, but I highly suggest you go to class as much as you can. I went to every class and I think that was one of the reasons I was able to do well. She also verbally says/explains more info you should know or that is helpful that is not on the slides, but her slides are pretty comprehensive. There are lecture assignments you need to be present for in lectures and many people missed these because they were sometimes during random/unpredictable lectures. Some of our lecture assignments were also just canvas quizzes before exams. She dropped 3/10 lecture assignments which was nice. She is a great professor and you just need to be prepared to take the time to memorize. If you don't understand a concept, her office hours are really helpful and she is always willing to help. There are always a couple of points of extra credit on each exam, but some of the true-false and even multiple choice can be tricky. I recommend slowing down and going over the true false multiple times. The written portion of the exams always has a concept she emphasized or spent more time on. The final exam was all multiple-choice and pretty fair in my opinion. Overall a really interesting class with an amazing professor!!

I took Dr. Fletcher for both BSCI170 and BSCI207 and he rocks !! Very fair exams that can be studied for easily by reviewing course materials and his practice questions. He’s very responsive and approachable, and is clearly so smart and an engaging lecturer even when teaching subjects that involve tons of info. Also super helpful that all of his lectures are recorded and you’ll always know well ahead of time if there will be a graded in-class group activity
Incredibly harsh midterm grader, no transparency with his students, overall terrible teacher. Sucks that the other sections got it easy when we are stuck with him.
Great teacher, not easy class, the recent reviews are very accurate, a MAJOR tip: study her slides for exams, and re watch any topic you don't fully understand.

Dr. F is a really cool guy and is very passionate about what he's lecturing on. You can tell he really wants you to learn and that the class is very important to him. He has you use TopHat for participation (but it's 50 guaranteed points for going to lecture). The lab and the lecture are being separated next semester into BSCI331 and BSCI332, so I'm sorry for those of you that don't get the lab to count toward your grade. I like reading the textbook just because that's the type of person I am, but it definitely prepares you for lecture. Only reason I'm giving a 4/5 is because he falls really behind on grading missed TopHat questions and slides aren't accessible through ELMS, only through TopHat.

I loved this class and Dr. Butts! I'm a bio major so I was pretty nervous going in - I have 0 neuro experience. But Dr. Butts made everything super digestible and his interest in the subject def shines through and makes it a pretty interesting class to study for. Don't get me wrong - you do have to study well. For each exam, I watched each lecture recording, took some good notes, did his review questions (which give a pretty good gauge of the exam questions), and went to his review session (not rly necessary) - doing all that allowed me to average around a 95 on all the exams, including the final. Yes, you have to put in the time, but everything is clear, organized, and learnable. He also makes it clear that he wants you to do well - he is willing to meet outside of class/office hours if you can't make the scheduled office hours / review sessions. Also, he does 5 group worksheets, which is a guaranteed 100/100 each as long as you complete it. The weekly quizzes are also easy to get consistent 9/10 and 10/10s on. Overall, I enjoyed this class a lot and really like Dr. Butts as a professor. Def reccomend!

I believe everything in this class is fair. Dr. Wu is one of the most supportive and nicest professors I've ever had at UMD. She truly cares about her students, and she's always happy to answer any question you have. Getting an A in this class is very doable as long as you keep up with the class materials (DON'T CRAM), complete the assignments on time, and ask for help when needed. There is an abundance of office hours available, whether that's Dr. Wu's or the TA's. I find attending both very helpful. I suggest asking Dr. Wu about specific questions regarding the lectures and asking the TA questions about the HW assignments, since they're the ones grading them. Piazza is also available for frequently asked questions among your classmates (both the TA and Dr. Wu are active most of the time to respond to any questions). If you're solely relying on learning the content through attending lectures, then it may be a challenging class to earn good grades on the exams. I recommend pre-learning or reviewing the material before the lecture (all lecture slides of all topics are posted in ELMS) through any AI software, and use the lecture time to jot down anything else that Dr. Wu mentioned and solidify any topics. Just learning the material is not enough to be successful in the class, as many questions on the exam are application based, but the HW assignments and the quizzes help prepare you. The quizzes are not timed as well. In terms of midterms, there are three midterms, and one is dropped. The third midterm was technically the final, but it's cumulative with new content. The exams are also open notes, but they have to be a physical copy of your notes. You can print a digital copy of your notes or handwrite them. There is a lot of information in each topic, so I suggest not cramming for the class and being familiar with the content. If you have everything in your notes, also familiarize yourself with where everything is, as one of the biggest challenges of the exam is finishing on time. In all her exams and a few HW assignments, there are extra credit opportunities. For the first midterm, she allows the student to earn some points back by doing a reflection about what went well, what didn't go well, and how to prepare for the next exam. You don't get all of your points back, but some. There are a lot of quizzes and HW being dropped as well (but refer to your syllabus. At the end of the semester, there's an extra credit assignment where you find a group of people to make a presentation about a recent research paper that's related to the class content. The presentation can be either in-person or online. Additionally, you can earn extra credits by asking questions in person after the presentation or by posting your questions alongside the online ones. Overall, the curriculum really shows how Dr. Wu wants her students to succeed in this class. The way the class is structured helped me puzzle together why scientists took certain steps in the experiments. I highly recommend taking this class with Dr. Wu.

PLEASE take her. yes, obv you need to put in effort if you want an A, but professor stump is on your side and wants you to succeed. lecture can be a bit boring sometimes and might feel slow but its honestly fine bc she has so many resources to help u succeed outside of lecture. i met with her 1:1 multiple times and those meetings were incredibly helpful. the one thing i wish she did is record lectures bc sometimes when studying the scanned notes can get a little confusing if you dont remember the exact context. the exams are really straightforward and i never got anything lower than an A. homework is online and is a good grade bump too. also def go to GSS if you can because those sessions were v helpful for working thru confusing concepts. basically if you have to take this class, take professor stump!

I have come to learn that labs are ALWAYS extremely uncoordinated and not in relation to lecture at all (very rarely will there be a crossover of material). The main assignments consist of the pre lab quiz, actual lab procedure, post lab, lab report, and reflection quizzes. None of the assignments are that difficult just tedious and sometimes don't relate to the lab (like the post lab questions in the manual). Also, highly recommend you study for the reflection quizzes because they will send your grade DOWN if you get one wrong (usually 2 or 3 questions so one question wrong is like a 50% or 60%). The biggest thing for me this semester was the grading. It is almost the end of the semester and lab reports from the very beginning of October have not been graded. Additionally, the TAs like to take points off for ANYTHING. Thank god grade scope lets you resubmit so just make sure you check over all of the requirements in there and in the module for that week to not miss stupid points. All of the TAs grade very differently (ex: I forgot to add something to the title page on two separate lab reports and one TA took points off and another did not). The lab is really not that bad. I had an alright TA who tended to divide the procedure into groups so we could get it done, share answers, and leave faster. I stayed till the actual lab ending time only once or twice. So far out of the labs I have taken, this has been the easiest one. But, everything other than that (like online and assignments) is unorganized, last minute, and unfair. It is an enormous amount of work for it being 1 credit. It is manageable, but it is highly annoying that it's more work that half of my other classes. It's funny that I have never even met the lab coordinator, yet she gets 1 star. Pray for a good TA and ask questions. Mine was pretty responsive over email. Have fun.

One of the most disorganized courses i have ever taken. prelabs were near impossible to get 10's on cause some of them had questions about sigfigs and others had q's tht had no answers just clickable buttons and u had to just guess what was being asked. DO THE EXTRA CREDIT ON BLACKBOARD IF U WANT TO GET AN A.

she is so smart, kind, funny, and beautiful. she made orgo so much more manageable and is challenging but fair in the best way. she’s so cool. for notes, she provides lecture guides can be downloaded to an ipad or printed beforehand so that you follow along with her instead of scrambling to write everything down yourself, which makes it so much easier to absorb everything. the filled out lecture guides also leave you with the best study resources ever. she also records lectures which is unique for the chem department and so nice!! and did i mention that she’s so smart and funny and beautiful and cool and awesome

As a 1 credit course, this lab is a lot more work than I believe 1 credit should be offering. Not only is there 3 hour lab once a week, but the post-lab questions, post-lab worksheets, studying for TAQs, and completing pre-labs often takes me 3 hours total to finish. My time in Friedman’s class was the epitome of having a professor who does the bare minimum. She might be a good professor for other chemistry classes, but I do not think she was organized enough for Chem 271. It felt like she was balancing more than she should. The most annoying part about this class has to be the homework. Also, she focuses on a lot of MCAT/medical topics in this class, which I find annoying because I don't intend to take the MCAT but I guess could be helpful for pre-med students.

Chem272 was probably the most time-consuming lab I have taken, but it was definitely not the worst. The worst part of this course is the lab reports each week that can take a long time, but once you get the hang of them, they arent too bad. If you need help, there are many office hours available, and the piazza was also helpful. You are given all of the resources you need to complete the lab reports. The lab reports can be graded a little harshly, with points being taken off for tiny things (get the hang of sig figs and error reporting early!). With this, don't be scared because the average for my semester was an 89.9%, and there was a pre-set curve in the syllabus, which is very generous. I was also very sick for one of the labs, and I really appreciated that I had no issues with a makeup assignment and I didn't feel like my grade suffered because I was absent. The midterm and final are very fair, and I highly recommend going to review sessions for them. For in lab, you work in groups and the lab instructions were sometimes confusing at first, but you figure it out. A lot of the labs took 2 hours or almost the whole time, but this can depend on your group and other things. I actually felt that I knew what was going on after doing each lab report, and some of the labs were really interesting. While taking this lab I was kinda annoyed because of the lab reports each week, but looking back it was probably one of my favorites that I took the most out of.

No exams and standards-based grading. Those are the primary reasons people flock to take Dr. Marsh, and for good reason. Most assignments can be resubmitted until the end of the semester, and you know exactly where you stand for most of the class. There are pitfalls in the philosophy, but overall, it was a nice change of pace compared to most of the classes I've taken. Dr. Marsh is a very chill professor, and he clearly has good experience in computer security. Unfortunately, I don't think he's the best lecturer. There's a reason attendance reportedly got as low as about 5 people some classes: people just didn't see a reason to keep going. For personal reasons, I didn't go to lectures in October. It's not like class performance suffered very much in spite of this, as a majority of the class are getting A's, if the ELMS statistics are anything to go by. I think it's mostly a presentation issue, as while there are (optional) exercises worked through live in class, I never really understood anything based off of the lectures. Live coding is a hard act to pull off effectively, and I don't think live demonstrations are Dr. Marsh's strongsuit. I feel like class periods were much more effective when they were essentially just office hours, as Dr. Marsh seemed much better at answering individual and specific questions about assignments. I'm conflicted because I see what Dr. Marsh is trying to do, but I think there needs to be more supplemental material (maybe a whiteboard program with a drawing tablet to illustrate the point of the coding exercises) to really make the lectures work. The nature of the build-it document resubmission should have been more clear (for context, build-it is designing a basic client-server architecture in C with all compiler security helpers turned off, and break-it consists of finding and exploiting a vulnerability in another group's submission). Dr. Marsh stated that the initial submission was due December 2nd, and that resubmissions would be available until the day before the final challenge problems were released. However, resubmissions weren't allowed to address vulnerabilities not addressed in the original submission, as we would have had an opportunity to look at other groups' build-it documents during the break-it phase. I think that's fine in general, but it wasn't explicitly stated in the syllabus or project description, so I believed that resubmissions just needed to correspond to the implementation submitted on December 2nd. It was a problem for my group, as for the 5 vulnerabilities we included, 2 of them were deemed invalid in our first submission, which resulted in an R (we needed an M or better on the EMRN scale to get a B or better in the class). We got it regraded to an M based on the criteria outlined for resubmissions (which a TA sent in a Piazza reply rather than any sort of official announcement), but things really should have been more clear from the start. Speaking of clarity, the projects. There's value in keeping certain things ambiguous, but I think the cryptography project in particular was a bit too vague. I couldn't really figure out what I needed to do from the project description, and I mainly figured out what to do by corresponding with others (corresponding with others is not an academic integrity violation in Dr. Marsh's eyes, though sharing implementation details is of course). It didn't help that to start with, the Gitlab repository for the project only has the README, and all of the ciphertext streams (64K in total, so not large files) are in ELMS. A bit more clarity, and maybe an example for the expected output of task 1 at least, would be helpful. Additionally, not particularly related to clarity, project 1 is kind of a rude awakening for many people. From what I can tell, the last time many people in the class did C was CMSC216. It's not much code, and it's free if you live and breathe assembly, but it relies on really understanding the stack layout of a compiled C program. The class has several challenge problems, which are essentially just write-ups. Honestly, I kind of enjoyed them. They're kind of what you put into them, and due to my internal need to answer each of them as thoroughly as I could, I did a lot of research for many of them, so I'd say I learned a fair bit. They're not going to give you expertise in any particular topic or anything, but for a class focused on the breadth of computer security, I would say these assignments did their job. Please just do them throughout the semester as intended. Procrastination was not my friend, so I didn't just barely get an A, but I barely passed as well. Overall, if you can get into this class, you should be fine if you have any sort of self-control. I have my issues, but given the structure and grading scheme of this class, they are far from deal breakers.

This is the hardest CS course at this university. I thought I could handle it, but by the end of the semester, I was broken as a student. I sacrificed so much. I stopped having hobbies. I stopped exercising. I stopped hanging out with friends. I stopped attending all my classes except for CMSC417. I experienced a depressive episode after spending 40+ hours on Project 4 just to get 25/100. CMSC417 was the only thing that mattered. That being said—I do recommend this course. CMSC417 is extremely useful, and the knowledge/skills you gain are worth gold. You will understand exactly how the Internet is structured. You will understand everyday protocols. You will understand exactly how wireless works, and so much more. I wish I could take it again just to truly master the content. This course is an experience. ADVICE: - Learn to take notes quickly. Bobby's lectures are hard to follow and fast paced, and (good) external resources are scarce. - Ask questions during lecture. Bobby will insult and humiliate you if he thinks the question is dumb, but it doesn't matter. You must understand the content. - Review and organize your notes after class. You only have enough time in lecture to loosely scribble down concepts and details. - Ask questions on Piazza. Bobby will literally stay up til 4:00am answering them. - Use office hours. Bobby is very happy to spontaneously hold OH at unscheduled hours, and he tends to be more generous with past exam answers to those who show up. I didn't attend the TA office hours, so I can't comment on those. - Start projects the day they are released. (You won't take this advice seriously, and you will suffer.) - Pick your group members wisely. You cannot succeed without them. This course will make you truly understand what it means to work together on a single codebase. Good luck. Fall 2024

Childs is great at lecturing and I really got a lot out of this class. It definitely helped me get more comfortable with algorithm design and proofs. Lectures were fairly fast-paced since we had a lot of material to cover, but he was always happy to clarify any questions people had. Lectures stuck fairly close to the textbook, which was also a good reference if something wasn't clear. Typically lectures would introduce some problem, then we would discuss an algorithm for solving it, prove correctness and analyze time complexity. There were five problem sets throughout the semester, with the lowest one dropped. Each one was fairly difficult, consisting of a five or so problems. We had one midterm and one final. The midterm was was fairly straightforward I thought, but with one tricky question. The main challenge was the time crunch. Everyone was writing frantically until the end. The average on the midterm was a 60% or so. The final was similar in difficulty, but had a little more time to work with. The average was a 72%, so a bit better than the midterm. Both exams we were given a number of practice problems. The class is typically curved, though I don't know what the cutoffs were. Overall if you are comfortable with proofs and putting a lot of time into this class, it is definitely worth taking. If you aren't really interested in the subject or you have a busy courseload already, probably best to avoid.
Super knowledgeable about this field, and also treats students really kindly. He's understanding of a lot of situations, and the exams were also easy. Highly recommend!

Why did she make this course go from an easy 1 credit asynch meme to this tedious shit we have to keep up with weekly. thumbs DOWN because noone needs a college class to learn python lol

However, the homework and exercises are often vague, and the supplementary materials don’t really help clarify things. The coding itself isn’t too hard if you're good at Python, but the biggest challenge is figuring out what the assignments are asking, since the modules and lecture content don’t always align. Communication is also an issue as TAs often don’t respond to emails, and their grading can be confusing because they rarely leave detailed comments. Even when you email about a grade, it may take multiple follow-ups before they explain what went wrong. Also, discussion is optional; half the time, the TAs aren't even there. The class isn’t terrible, but unless you’re solid in Python and comfortable self-teaching, you might benefit more from an in-person version of this course.

I enjoyed the content of the class but you can get that with Professor Duffy. Please do so if you can. I have gone to Prof Duffy in-person class just to understand the material better. I passed the class with an A+ because of Duffy. Mrs. Shah's structure is HORRENDOUS. She doesn't do anything about the students who expect you to do all the work. She sends out emails addressing complaints and says that she will reach out to them but NOTHING CHANGES and they can slack off and still pass. We have mandatory meetings with the TAs and this is where you have a check-in on the status of your project. Her TAs do all the work for her and she reads Duffy's slides word for word. The two good reviews are because they didn't have to deal with bad teammates on top of the unnecessary confusion and stress. You will mostly be teaching yourself or seeking for guidance the whole semester.
My grade got better after I stopped showing up to her lectures and read the textbook on my own. I think that speaks for itself.

Dr. Ebrahimian is a very professional guy and a talented lecturer. He will aptly answer any question to make sure everything is understood. Math 141 is a difficult course, however, and it's important to stay on top of topics by doing as much practice as you can (assigned homework problems and worksheets).

Wiseley Wong is the goat. Although he is a chalkboard lecturer, his handwriting is very clear and he only writes on the middle ones so everyone can see. He explains concepts very well and always tells you what will be on the quizzes. 15% for 3 exams, 30% final, 15% quizzes, and 10% matlab. Everything was very fair, the true/false questions are a pain but they prepare you for the final! He answers questiosn very well and is not afraid to call people out for talking really loud in his lectures! And no curve because his exam scores are so high, midterm averages are around 80%.

Whoever gave him 5 stars for 241 I kinda see their point in that he teaches to make sure you fully understand everything, BUT the way he goes about it makes it not worth it at all. He basically forgets that there is a way to both maximize student understanding and success, because he only goes for comprehension, while you suffer with the grade. The 43% average on the first exam reflects that, but it's okay because he curved it by 2% to a 45%!!. I agree that he was a good lecturer who spoke clearly and gave good advice while breaking down complex topics. However, his exams are extremely unfair because even while understanding the topics (not just straight memorization), the questions are STILL challenging. It honestly goes beyond calc 3 and tests how good you are at time management, plus crazy application (long word problems combining multiple subtopics) since exams only leave enough time for one to recognize how to do it at a first look and then complete it. Once you're stuck, you've got to move on and hope there's time at the end!! Even 4 minutes can be life changing cause on the final I finished with 26 seconds to spare. To study for his class, I skip the straightforward problems in the textbook and go straight to the application section because he will ALWAYS put problems in context and test your comprehension. If you like taking math to the next level out of interest for yourself, then I would see how you would kind of like him, but if you're just trying to survive, then please don't take him.

Great lecturer, made topics easy to understand, exams were pretty easy (exam averages were B+/A- for all three midterms). No required work in discussion sections. There are 4 Matlab projects but the lowest score is dropped making it essentially 3 Matlab projects. Matlab projects are auto-graded instead of manually graded which I preferred but this did lead to a few frustrating moments with the autograder not working as expected (nothing that couldn't be sorted out by emailing Stefan ofc). Overall I'd recommend!

Dr. Gruber has basically every positive trait you want in a teacher. He's very approachable, has good notes, paces his class well, and grades sensibly (maybe even too leniently lol). Lectures are recorded, notes are posted, good study guides/practice problems are given, and he's just very pleasant to talk to in general. He really does care about all his students and how well they've learned the material. If Gruber is teaching a class you want, his section(s) should be your top choice without a second thought.

DO NOT TAKE MATH401 with Vadim!!! He is extremely disorganized, makes exams unnecessarily difficult, and does not even follow the course topic. To recap, the madness of this course started when Vadim accidentally gave his practice exam as the actual exam for our second midterm. This happened because Vadim was absent for the exam, and incorrectly sent the sub the practice exam instead. You would think this was a huge help for all the students, except it was the complete opposite. This practice exam contained problems which involved heavy use of irrational numbers, which made questions designed to take 15 minutes, instead take 45. The first problem on the exam alone took 45 minutes (assuming you could even solve it), and this was only one of the ten questions on the exam. The following class, Vadim carried on with lecture, and did not even acknowledge any of what had happened in the previous class. Then, students complained about this at the end of the class, and no announcements followed. In the final class of the semester, we finally discovered with further questioning that the second midterm would not be part of our grade, and the final would be 50% of our course grade (yes, 50!!!). The final, of course, was obscenely difficult as well. Problems featured complex numbers, and, again, irrational numbers. No college student should be expected to be able to finish an exam like this in 2 hours. Once again, Vadim was not there to administer the exam, and had a sub do it instead. Additionally, Vadim did not properly announce to the class, that calculators were allowed. This meant that some of the class did not even get access to a calculator on the exam, when it was, of course, extremely helpful for the excessively difficult numbers on the exam. I would be impressed if even a third of the class was able to get through the entire exam. What makes this class so irritating, is that it had no reason to even be frustrating like this in the first place. Instead of covering applications of linear algebra (like the course title would suggest), the course was instead just a review of MATH240, except with painfully disgusting/tedious exam problems, which you don't get exposure to in class or homeworks. MATH240 somehow discussed more applications of linear algebra than this course. MATLAB was not even used one time in this class, and we spent the entire semester tediously row reducing, and finding determinants and eigenvectors. Vadim is WAY too disorganized to teach, and the students are the ones who pay the price for this. Even if the course title interests you and you're not afraid of a challenge, do not take this class, because you're not gonna learn anything whatsoever about applications linear algebra, and you're just gonna spend a whole semester tediously solving problems meant for a computer.

Amin is overall a very strong teacher. He knows a lot about his content, and most of his explanations and proofs are not terrible to follow (they are hard because the course is hard, but he explains it well and makes it as easy to understand as a course like this possibly could be). He really likes when students give answers or ask questions, and I do think his enjoyment of the content makes the class more enjoyable. He is also super helpful in office hours - the homework gets super tough, but if you make an appointment with him he will clear up any questions you have. His grading structure placed a big emphasis on homework - which personally I liked, because it means your grade is far more dependent on the work you do consistently each week, and you can get help with it, instead of having your entire grade boil down to how well you do on a few timed exams. The grading structure with midterms and finals also ensures that if either your midterm average or your final exam score is high enough, the other will also be very high. So overall the class was hard, and he does fall into a classic college level math teacher pattern of talking at the board for the entire class, but I thought he was a good teacher with friendly policies.

Great guy. His lectures are well-structured, if fast, and he explains things clearly, going into great depth on each topic. Homeworks are challenging but manageable, and they push you to think deeper about the concepts. Exam averages tend to be low, but there are plenty of extra credit opportunities to help you boost your grade. He answers any questions you may have very thoroughly and doesn't make you feel stupid, and he's also willing to talk about concepts beyond the scope of the class if you're interested. It's clear he's extremely knowledgeable and passionate about what he does.

Apparently, this was his first semester teaching 406. I wouldn't have guessed - we just go over proofs in class and he is pretty good at explaining everything going on. If you do zone out and stop following a proof, he usually goes over the important conclusions at the start of the next class anyway. We have homework posted every Friday due the next Friday and that's pretty much it except for exams. The homeworks are good practice for the exams and don't typically take too long. The two midterms were only four problems that were directly related to what we had covered in class and intuitive, especially because he will give a selected list of problems from the homework to study and solutions to them. He is always willing to give a hint in an email or in class if you are stuck on a problem on the homework too. I haven't been to office hours since I haven't had to but he's pretty chill in class. Assuming he doesn't suddenly get really mean, I thought he was awesome! Learned a lot of cool stuff and none of it was much pressure!

Panos is one of the best math professors I have had at UMD. He obviously cared so much more about us understanding the concepts of the class and enjoying the proofs than "testing" us. All of our exams were take home and we were able to work on homework in groups. I couldn't recommend him more for this class.
Teaching style is fine. Let his 2 favorite students go to the bathroom together during his final exam for about 10 minutes, so you'll probably have an A+ if he likes you.

He not a good, not even decent professor. His lecture slides are mostly useless brining in concepts from engineering level courses that will not even show up on your exam. Eventually wasting your time. There is nothing to prepare you for the exams like old exams or practice questions besides the ones he picks from expert ta which are mostly too difficult for the course level. His curve is almost non existent for a class with exam averages that are F and D. Lecture is useless honestly since he just yaps and reads off formulas. Exam questions are weirdly worded and structured requiring you to have a proficient level of physics understanding. Quizzes are as bad as the exams. Home works take hours to complete even including knowledge we have not learned or relevant to the class. In general by any means avoid this man, even if you have to postpone the class a semester or so. He might be nice but hes not built to teach lower level of physics courses that only require basic algebra and understanding. People giving him 4 stars might be people that have previously taken physics so the class seemed easy but if I could I would give him 0 stars.

Dr. Kim is a great professor! I don't know what these other reviews are talking about. Yes, he has an accent. So what? He does explain well, and he genuinely cares about how well his students do. He makes himself very accessible with multiple office hours and quick responses via email. He does the coolest demos ever! Sometimes I felt more like I was watching a magic show than sitting in physics lecture. I was actually excited to go to class, and I don't even like physics! Just go to class! He even made the class before every exam a review session and told us exactly what to study. If you go to class, pay attention, and do what he says you will do well.

Skill level: Physics is the most difficult subject for me and I will never understand it. I genuinely did orgo practice problems as a break from studying for this class. The only reason why I probably didn’t get a 0 on the midterms was because my dried teardrops on the exams made the guy feel bad. As for Buehrle himself, he seemed like a pretty chill and nice guy, trying to engage the class as much as he could. The ExpertTA and TopHat homeworks do take a bit of time, so I wouldn’t wait until the very last minute to do them. I did learn a lot more from them than the lectures, which often made no sense to me. I would try to put in as much effort into getting a good grade on those homeworks as you can because they really boosted my grade. The midterms were awful for me and I often did below average, even with the (generous) curve he gives. Even after the first two exams I felt lost on how to study for this class. However, for the final, I would highly recommend doing all the homework problems as similar, if not the exact same, questions appeared on the exam. I would also practice a lot of estimation problems as every exam had them. In terms of the lab, having a good group can really impact how long you’re in the lab and the amount of work everyone has to put in. Most of the labs took 2-4 weeks, so I would recommend staying in the lab to finish as much of the report as you can the first week and doing the rest outside of class, so the next few weeks you only have to attend for like a minute to sign the attendance sheet (depending on how chill your TA is). My TA didn't require us to stay in lab to do the practice problems, so no one ever really did them, which meant we could start on lab and leave early. They also didn’t grade the reports harsh, but Buehrle does adjust if any of the TAs do.

Cool guy but it's pretty obvious that he hates teaching this course. The best way to get to know him is to go to his office hours. He's a bit impatient and won't sugarcoat things when he explains concepts, but he knows what he's talking about. If you ask the right questions he can be very helpful. I personally highly recommend going to the TA office hours whenever you get the chance. They'll be more willing to hold your hand for a lot of these more complicated concepts and explain things in more intuitive ways (which I personally needed and I know a lot of students appreciated). While this course has a very generous curve and the assignments are a great buffer, the content itself can be very complicated depending on how well you want to understand it. Don't just brush off the content because it'll haunt you on the MCAT.

Why are people hating on her. She's genuinely the best physics professor I've had in my entire life. Her exams were really fair and straightforward. I think if you put into the effort needed, you will have a good grade.

This lab is pretty decent. Once you get the experiment going, it's pretty easy to see how the concepts from 260 apply, so it is beneficial in terms of providing a real-world example. However, the technicalities of the course can be confusing--how to use the random equipment they have set up each week, how to enter difficult formulas into the excel spreadsheets, how to calculate errors, etc. Overall, not that bad, but the explanations need to be a bit clearer on some things.

you learn nothing and pass because the curve is so heavy, going to class is completely useless but nobody else learns anything so you somehow end up fine. If you want to actually learn, avoid If you don't care and just need to pass, TAKE HIM

Chandra is a fantastic professor who really prioritizes student learning. The content is difficult, but the group problem solving sessions are super helpful and she provides exam and homework corrections which make learning the material more obtainable. Although I don't love that she only uses slides for lecture, they are helpful for review. Some combination of slides and working things out on the board would be even better.

I've had Dr Hall twice now. I liked him the first time (phys272) and I loved him the second tie (phys401). He's a good lecturer. His notes were very well organized, which is something I find extremely helpful in understanding the material. He also would use the discussion time to go over the answers to the homework, which was amazingly helpful. The tests for 401 were take home, which made it more about what you actually understand and less about what you can remember in an hour. He has definitely been my favorite physics professor.

Chacko's grading scheme is pretty fair. If you attain maximum points on the homework (14 assignments worth 2 points each, maximum points to earn is 20), get the one homework question completely correct on the midterm, and both homework questions completely correct on the final, then you get a C. He makes it clear from the get-go that getting an A is not an easy task. That said, if you work hard on the homework, it'll probably carry over the midterm. I felt like I did terribly on the midterm, maybe getting a C but bracing for worse, but I ended up getting an A. He engages the students in questioning during lecture to keep them active in coming up with physical reasoning or making observations about physical systems that lead to the course content he wants to deliver. His examples, while right out of the book, were still very helpful and usually presented with much more clarity than in the text. I think I learned more in this class than any other physics class I've had up to this point (and there are still things I should go back to review!). (And don't get me wrong - while I worked hard and think I should go back and study even more, I'm not an exemplary student. When Chacko said we should be working extra problems from the text, even should be reading the text, and said we should be reading extra textbooks, I was mildly terrified that that was what was expected of me if I was to ever succeed in physics. I mean, when do I get the time to do all this stuff? I think if you have good attention to the physics of classical systems, and good intuition about how systems should behave, then you'll do fine.)

Khurana is a really great professor. Really helps her students succeed in the class. Class consists of homework assignments, in class activities, two exams and the final, and r coding assignments. Overall very easy. The R Assignments sometimes can be annoying to do, but they are pretty easy, and are also gone over in discussion. Khurana wants the best for her students, and that was evident throughout the class. If you’re going to take STAT100, and she is available, definitely take it with her.

Not nearly as bad as the reviews here would suggest. Was admittedly a somewhat poor lecturer the first few weeks with convoluted examples, but definitely improved throughout the course of the semester. Homeworks also only have max 1 proof/theoretical question, the rest are mostly computational and not as hard as suggested. Honestly did not find exams 1 and 2 that hard, even with no prior Stats experience and moderate studying, going to class is key imo even people say otherwise. Zheng also listened to feedback, ended up curving midterms, and provided better material for exam 2. Overall not the best lecturer in the world and still makes things a little confusing at times but got better as the year went on and is an open and nice professor. Take everything else read here with a grain of salt

decent at explaining stuff, fair exams (median of 83/84 on the two midterms), final was a bit cooked (64% median), but he gave 5% extra credit to do some free summaries of some stat articles (literally 5% added to ur grade) and the cutoff for an A was a 90 so it's a pretty free class and i actually learned stuff cuz he's a decent lecturer. also uploads his slides and records lectures.

dont let this guy get tenure omg, he omitted so much integral material, no supports, no sigma algebras, straight into an oddly intuitive form of probability and had zero set theoretical background before delving into it.

Very interesting and funny professor in class! I really enjoyed his jokes, and he made the content quite interesting. I do wish he spent a little less time working on STAT410 material in the beginning of the semester, but other than that, I don't really see many problems with this professor!

Nice professor who makes a good effort to be accessible. Cares a lot about attendance and paying attention in class, so she made attendance part of the grade, and also heavily weighted the midterm and final (30% of the grade for each). Exams tend to have a few questions that are designed to trip you up, and often also drill you on specifics which can be a bit unfair. Overall, this class becomes tougher than it really should be.

Where do I even begin with Professor Shapiro? He is extremely disorganized and frantic when lecturing. It may seem like he is doing you a favor by posting his slides, but they are all pictures and like 100+ slides per class, which is ridiculous. You have to go to lecture to even have a chance to do well, but it doesn't help that much because he zooms through things extremely fast. If you email him with a question, he is very quick to respond and usually fixes errors in your favor, which is very appreciated, but the class was simply just a joke. His 3 homeworks were pointless, and the 2 associated quizzes were ridiculous, considering that if you got one question wrong, you already got a B. He was testing SimBio alternate assignments, and those were beyond stupid, frustrating, and simply just a waste of time. I felt like those hurt my grade more than anything and distracted you from what was actually important to him. His (3) exams are all very niche vocab and examples he mentions in lecture for .5 seconds, which is so ridiculous because he doesn't tell you that, and then you get the first exam and are like, well f*ck. He does allow a notecard for each exam and a 1 sided cheat-sheet for the final, so eventually you learn what he expects from you, but not after you tank the first exam. All around, as a person who was taking this for an easy NS credit, don't do it with him. None of the professors are great, but unless you are an ultimate try-hard or gifted in Bio, I haven't met a person who has done very well in this course.

This review is more for the course than Hans. You likely won't see him throughout the semester and will only ever communicate with him if you're absent. The course content was easy and mostly just busy work but your general experience will also depend on the TA and group members.

Nice guy, bad professor. His lectures are so incredibly boring and he explains concepts poorly and as if he is teaching a 300 level class. His tests have a lot of questions that are worded confusingly. He does drop your lowest of the 3 midterms. He gives a lot of "free points" which is about 30% of the grade but everything else is the exams. You'll need to read the textbook, watch lectures of other professors (which is linked on canvas), and study with friends to find any success in his class.

I never actually met this person. For BSCI171 you are assigned a random TA, who will make or break your lab experience. Personally, I loved my TA she was awesome and so chill and made the class not as dreadful as I thought it was going to be. Hopefully you will get a laid back and easy-going TA who will grade easily. Swarna Mohan I believe is just the BSCI171 lab coordinator/director you will only email Mohan if you are going to have to be absent for lab and they will assign you a make-up assignment. Or, if something goes wrong during lab I suppose. I also found lab to be a lot easier than bio (BSCI170) itself. The labs can be quite long and tedious but thy are only once a week, so I recommend taking it early in the week (like Monday's) to get it over with for the week. Outside of class I had post & pre lab quizzes, and some other random assignments. We also had a group project making a digital poster/presentation with our lab group that we were assigned in class. At the end of the semester (typically the last day of lab) there is a lab practical which isn't too hard where you have to demonstrate everything you've learned infront of your TA. Overall this class isn't too bad you just kind of have to suck it up do the work and get it over with.

I don't know why she has a 3-star rating; it should be like a 1. She's not aware of her class environment and just reads off lectures. She's basically getting paid to talk. DO NOT TAKE THIS DESPICABLE LADY WHO CAN'T TEACH UNLESS YOU WANT TO SUFFER.

Dr. Lombardi is a really amazing professor, there is just so much content in this class that you really have to put in a ton of work - especially if it doesn't come as naturally (me sadly). She posts panopto recordings of the lectures that saved my life when studying and she explains things pretty well. I definitely suggest taking her over any other professor - just be prepared for pretty tough exams and definitely use crash courses + stuff to help!

Genuinely one of the nicest and sweetest people I've seen at UMD, and an alright class overall. There's a lot of information covered in BSCI207, and she doesn't expect you to memorize it all, mostly just the general knowledge and idea. You do get a cheat sheet for each exam, longer units having a double-sided sheet (handwritten). Once again, she really wants you to succeed, and you should pay attention to the GAEs and review them for the free response. Exams aren't exactly easy because of the sheer amount of content, but it's doable if you review. There's no curve or exam drop like I've seen happen before, but we had three exams, and the final unit was 50% of the final.

Genuinely one of the worst professors I've ever had. Sometimes, the wording on her slides does not make sense to the point where I spend more time deciphering it than actually understanding the material. I've attended every single lecture, hoping that things would make sense to me if I went in person. Still, she literally reads off the slides and occasionally rephrases her points in different wording. Although the labs and her other assignments add as buffers to our grades, her exams are actually awful. I would honestly rather do an orgo2 exam than hers anytime. Almost everyone I know has either a C or a B in the class right now, and we don't know what to expect for her final at all because there's genuinely so much material she covers with very little time. Also, she doesn't curve so good luck with that.

Not the worst professor I've ever had, but I do agree with many of the other reviews. This class definitely had the heaviest workload of all my classes this semester, and not because it was hard. There was a lot of unnecessary busy work that didn't really deepen my understanding of the material or help me prepare for exams. The upside is that the PAKs are graded for completion and TAs tend to grade leniently on the lab assignments, so the busy work helps to pad your grade. In lab time, there are no assignments you have to complete and turn in for a grade, but some of your results or presentations might be needed for assignments you turn in later, so I'd recommend taking pictures of your results. We usually leave lab 30 min-1 hr early. Other than the exams, there are 2 other major grading assignments, which are part of the lab portion. These are the lab report and research poster presentation, both of which are really easy as long as you follow the rubric. Almost all the lab assignments are done as part of a group that gets chosen at the start of the semester, so make sure you pick your teammates wisely. I also disliked the flipped classroom format, where you watch recorded video lectures on your own time and do clicker questions in class. If I wanted to learn by staring at a screen, I'd have gone on YouTube instead of paying thousands in tuition. I'd recommend double speeding the videos. The clicker questions were graded on completion but most were kind of useless for the exam and we had to pay for PointSolutions. Besides clicker questions, the lectures consisted of talking about current scientific research or topics related to microbiology, like the 2025 US measles outbreak. These are nice to know but useless for the exams. I'd much prefer it if they were included in the additional reading section for those who are interested instead of presented during class time. Near the end of the semester, Dr. Buchner had a more traditional lecture style since we finished all the pre-recorded content. I took notes in these lectures, but a lot of it was him reading off of the slides. Dr. Buchner does record his in-person lectures but I've never watched them. Overall, lectures were useless for the exam, but I attended for the clicker points. There were 3 exams (2 midterms and a final), with the final worth the same amount of points as the midterms, but with more questions and cumulative. The exam content was all from the recorded video lectures (and traditional in-person lectures once those ran out) AND lab procedures. Studying the textbook was unnecessary. I wouldn't say the exams were unfair since all the content was covered in the class, but since Dr. Buchner didn't provide any study materials, many people didn't know what the exam format would be like. It was also his first semester doing an in-person exam instead of online, which may have contributed to the low averages. His exams include drawing diagrams, interpreting diagrams, short answer, some multiple choice, and logic questions (Ex: you have a procedure and you forget one of the steps; how does that affect the final results). If Dr. Buchner prints out a handout and goes over it in lecture, make sure to pay attention because it's going to be on the exam. Each exam has one free question thrown in, where you get points as long as you answer it sensibly. I studied for exams by rewatching the recorded video lectures, reading my notes, and looking over lab procedures. Dr. Buchner said he doesn't give out any previous exams, but that he won't stop students from sourcing them themselves. We couldn't do this since we were the first semester to have in-person exams with Dr. Buchner, but I would recommend finding previous in-person exams as study materials. Other notes: - I've heard that Dr. Tran had easier exams than Dr. Buchner. - Dr. Buchner seemed like a pretty chill guy when I talked to him. - If you've taken BSCI222, this class should be a breeze. - I don't think this class was harder than BSCI222, but it has more busy work. - I've heard that Dr. Buchner is lenient about extensions, as long as you email him before the assignment is due. - Dr. Buchner is strict about late work. - If Dr. Buchner provided practice exams and there wasn't so much busy work, this would be a free class. - I didn't learn as much about microbiology as I expected. If you're interested in microbiology as a subject, take BSCI283 instead.

Best prof ever, tries to make learning fun thru jokes. Only annoying part is clicker questions. He genuinely wants his students to succeed, and he doesn't change the exams from year to year. Get an old exam and you'll be fine. Will miss this class so much.

I may have to go against the grain here, but if you are taking this class with a lighter course load (that is, you are not taking it alongside MammPhys) and you are interested in pursuing neuroscience related research/internships, I would take it with Dr. Caras. This is typically not the case for many people, since this class is usually taken junior year and is a requirement for the Neurobio&Phys major. Although this class is difficult, you will definitely leave the class having understood the content at a much deeper level, relative to the other biology classes at UMD. Will your grade reflect it? Because of the sheer depth and memorization demands, you are bound to miss something while studying, so probably not. Compared to endocrinology and virology, which are both 400-level bio classes, this class was more difficult. It's not because the content itself is more difficult, it's that Dr. Caras requires that you understand these concepts mechanistically. Furthermore, this class is particularly difficult because the content you learn throughout the semester is compounding. If you don't really understand the electrochemical gradient (which is taught early on), the rest of the class is a struggle. Given that her class demands a lot more depth, here are the pros and cons of her teaching style: Pros: 1. Her slides have no "fat". There is no extra content, every single slide is important and fair game. In fact, if you think of her lecture/slides as a supplement for prereading and taking notes from the textbook, you will be in great shape. That's why this class is going to be difficult for someone taking a bunch of other classes. 2. She is generous with help on the graded in-class worksheets and regrade requests. 3. She is enthusiastic about the science (and about particular topics, which tend to show up on exams more). 4. Midterm averages increased through the semester (83, 84, 95 for Exams 1-3, respectively). 5. Slides are posted in advance. 6. Lots of extra credit (we had ~25 points of extra credit across the 4 exams). This must be a new addition to the course since other reviews said that she does not offer EC. Cons: 1. This semester she tended to finish her lectures early. This is sometimes good because then you have more time to ask questions; however, as other folks have mentioned here, that's 25-30 pages of content in about an hour of lecture. If you haven't done the reading (which happened to me several times), it's very difficult to keep up. I suppose that's why we have the pre-lecture textbook reading quizzes (which you could technically finish without having read the textbook, but then what's the point). 2. Final exam average was a ~75%. 3. No practice exams. You can try to compile the weekly worksheets to simulate a practice exam. The worksheets are quite similar to the practice exams, but about 25% easier. If you make comprehensive flash cards (mentioned below), you can bridge that knowledge gap and really master the content. 4. Slides that are posted are sometimes a little outdated (and the additional diagrams are helpful). 5. Readings can be quite long, a good idea would be to split them over 3 days. So you came here to decide whether you should take 330 with Cliff or Anwar. Well I'm here to tell you that you should just choose one that has a better schedule for you. Any sort of "coding" question you get in a quiz or exam is some permutation of a function you implemented for a relevant project. So if you're not a GPT warrior and actually implemented the functions by understanding what its asking for, those questions should be a breeze. I'll be the one to say it...OCaml is really not that bad to understand (cry about it yall just work with any code that isn't written like a pseudocode). The syntax is really trivial to grasp especially if you have worked with "let" expressions in JS. HOWEVER, the functional programming aspect of it is where it gets tricky. But once you have enough practice with the first two projects (really only the first project because it is designed to teach you how functional programming in OCaml works), you will spend less time worrying about the language itself rather implementing the necessary concepts into the projects. You will *lightly* go over Rust programming towards the last 20% of the course which is a much more traditional language, and is primarily used to teach concepts on type safety. All in all, it is very manageable. I'm still salty that I didn't perform up to my potential in this course because I felt like I really understood what was taught but sold on the exams because I'm a nervous wreck and tend to blank out during them. Use the practice they give you (exams and quizzes dating back to the days where CS wasn't a 40,863 student per class major) and redo them till you can recognize the type of questions on the exam and can get instantly started on solving them. Also, Friday discussions were not it because wtf but they're worth it if you need the additional practice and sometimes you have to go because they give quizzes (they'll tell you when they are so don't worry). So go to discussion. Or don't.

This is a review after taking the course in Summer 2026 (June 2 to July 25). It's an 8-week course assigning about 1 to 2 hours of content per day (excluding weekends, holidays, and days before exams). Content mainly consists of videos, with occasional interactive Python notebooks and PDFs of lecture notes. The videos are pre-recorded sessions of Teli switching between PowerPoint slides and an overhead view of him writing on paper. They walk through the math behind foundational machine learning algorithms, like computing entropy and information gain for decision trees or tracing partial derivatives for backpropagation. Grading breakdown: 25% homework, 25% projects, 25% midterm, 25% final. Homeworks are ELMS Canvas quizzes with no time limit, usually allowing 2 to 3 attempts. Answers unlock after the final submission. Projects involve working with notebooks to implement core logic behind classifiers, regressors, and neural nets, essentially building a basic Scikit-learn-like backend. The setup expects you to test code by running python.exe commands through a Conda environment, which can feel clunky compared to using a modern IDE. Some code may also need fixing due to outdated syntax or dependencies. It's generally easy to get 100% on all projects and homework, plus some optional extra credit on Project 3 that can add up to 1.25% to your final grade. As others have noted, most of the weight falls on the midterm and final. About half the practice exam content matched what appeared on the actual tests. The rest depends on your study coverage. Some 20- to 30-point questions may catch you off guard if you haven’t reviewed all concepts, algorithm traces, math derivations, or the optional textbook (ciml-v0_9-all). Overall, the course is structured and well-paced for 8 weeks. While some topics or variations are trimmed or glossed over due to time constraints, which the professor openly acknowledges, it’s clear he enjoys the material and puts in consistent effort to explain each concept in a way that builds understanding for the viewer.

I agree that the other reviews have been too harsh. My impression of the class is that the workload is high, but you will learn a lot. I felt that the grading was lenient despite the high workload. The majority of the workload comes from the reading homeworks before each class. They are advertised to be 1.5 hours, but I regularly spent more than that on them. They are also not easy, and you can’t expect to get all the questions right. The clicker questions are similar to the reading homeworks, but they are more lenient since multiple answers can be correct. Unfortunately, I noticed that after doing the reading homeworks, the lectures were a bit stale since they mostly rehashed the content covered in the homeworks. The 4 projects have one of the most lenient late penalties I’ve ever seen, with 2.5% off per day late. Overall they were not too bad, comparable to the workload of CMSC420 projects. The last 2 projects were different since they used an established codebase. I spent a lot of time on those projects jumping around the codebase and trying to figure out what was going on. The exams were challenging and similar to the reading homeworks and clicker questions. The final exam was surprising compared to other finals in that there were almost no “gimmes” that I could answer quickly and move on. Instead of asking “do you remember this definition/formula/question”, most of them looked like “can you use the underlying concept and apply it to new situations”. For me the HW and clicker questions, along with the practice exams, were the best way to prepare. Because of that, I think you gotta lock in the entire semester, more so than other courses, to be able to digest and understand the questions at a reasonable pace. I don’t think cramming by reading through the slides and memorizing formulas would be very successful for these exams. Overall, I’d say this is one of the harder CS electives out there. The ceiling for workload is high in that there’s a lot of content and you can end up spending a lot of time on it. Even without reaching that ceiling, I think it’s possible to get a good grade with the curves.
